FewStepRL: Fine-tuning Few-step Diffusion Models with
Reinforcement Learning

 

Haitao Lin1,⋆,†, Minsi Ren2,⋆, Yang Li1,†,
Xingtong Ge1, Zheyuan Hu1, Peiyan Hu2,3, Tailin Wu2,‡
Affiliation: 1Tencent Hunyuan, 2 Westlake University, 3 University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

⋆Equal contribution; †Project Leader; ‡Corresponding author: wutailin@westlake.edu.cn

Contents

1 Introduction

Diffusion models and their flow-matching counterparts generate data by integrating a learned transport from noise to samples, and have become a dominant approach to image and video synthesis (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021b; Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Rombach et al., 2022; Esser et al., 2024). Because the learned field is accurate only locally, sampling typically takes tens of network evaluations (Song et al., 2021a).

Few-step models remove most of this cost by learning the transport over long intervals directly. Consistency models and MeanFlow, which models the average velocity over an interval, and on-policy distilled flow maps such as DMD and AnyFlow generate in one to four evaluations (Song et al., 2023; Geng et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2026; Yin et al., 2024b; Gu et al., 2026).

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a standard post-training method for diffusion models. Fine-tuning against reward models of human preference, text rendering or composition measurably improves the outputs (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025a; Xue et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026a). This gain, however, typically requires samples from the current policy at every iteration and must be protected against reward hacking, in which the policy exploits the reward model instead of improving.

With a many-step sampler, these rollouts typically account for most of the time and memory of training, and more so for long video sequences. A few-step model shrinks this cost, but it models an average velocity over an interval, whereas the RL objectives above are built for an instantaneous velocity or for the transitions of a many-step sampler. Applied directly, they leave open which network evaluation should be differentiated, how the reference policy should be evaluated, and which parts of the interval are trained. Prior work typically resolves these choices for one objective at a time (Huang et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026b); what is, to our knowledge, missing is a systematic way to adapt RL objectives to few-step models. Figure 1 illustrates the effect of leaving them unresolved. Substituting the average velocity of a distilled few-step model for the instantaneous velocity required by FlowGRPO, AWM and DiffusionNFT, i.e., applying the original objective to the distilled model without modification, gives a lower best GenEval2 than the adapted objective derived in this paper in each of the three cases.

This paper builds one in three phases (Figure 2), namely a transformation, a decomposition and an adaptation. The transformation maps each objective to xx-space. Under a linear noise schedule, a velocity defines an affine map between noise levels, so each objective we consider can be expressed through a common policy prediction, at the clean end by default and at an explicitly marked level for transition or flow-map objectives. In xx-space, objectives stated over densities, velocities or rewards become directly comparable. The decomposition splits the loss gradient. The gradient of every objective we consider is the sum of a self-regression term, which keeps the policy close to a reference, and a reward-augmentation term, which contains the reward, so that, at the gradient level, a method reduces to a choice of anchors and weights. The adaptation extends the anchors to few-step models. We show how each anchor is computed from a few-step model, either at the end of its transport or along the tangent of the trajectory, with the instantaneous velocity recovered from the network itself, as in MeanFlow, or from an auxiliary network, as in DMD.

All methods share one codebase, which is represented by a single training step with several method-specific stages, namely rollout, reward and advantage, anchors and weights, and loss (plus auxiliary fitting and the refresh of the old policy), where each method overrides only the hooks in which it differs (§5). The methods are therefore compared under shared rollout, reward and evaluation code, and a new variant is specified mainly by its anchors and weights. Experimentally, we compare seven implementations on image generation with an AnyFlow-distilled SD3.5-Medium (Stability AI, 2024; Gu et al., 2026), under a non-differentiable OCR reward and a differentiable mixed reward, and on video generation with an AnyFlow-distilled Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B (Team Wan et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2026); we further test whether the fine-tuned few-step models improve when sampled with more steps.

The contributions of this paper are as follows.

  • •

    A general view. After the transformation to xx-space, the gradients of the RL objectives considered here share one decoupled form, the sum of a self-regression term and a reward-augmentation term, so that their gradients differ only in their anchors and weights.

  • •

    A systematic adaptation to few-step models. Each of these anchors can be computed from an average-velocity model at the end of the transport or along its tangent, which yields few-step versions of FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL within one modular codebase.

  • •

    Empirical guidance with experimental analysis. Where the reward is differentiable and its gradient affordable, reward-gradient-based methods are the most effective in our experiments, and ReFL alone is a strong baseline. Otherwise, group-advantage methods apply. Among them, DiffusionNFT-style methods generally reach high rewards in relatively few iterations, even when one iteration is expensive, and DMD-based variants are faster per iteration on image but slower on video, depending on the relative cost of forward and backward passes, and often coincide with larger held-out degradation. Additional inference steps bring little aggregate improvement in generation quality, while visual gains appear in selected outputs with more sampling steps than training.

2 Background

Diffusion and flow-based generators.

Diffusion models learn to reverse a fixed noising process (Ho et al., 2020); score-based models cast this reversal as a reverse-time SDE whose probability-flow ODE gives a deterministic sampler, of which DDIM is a discrete instance (Song et al., 2021b; Song et al., 2021a). Flow matching and rectified flow instead regress the velocity of a prescribed interpolation between noise and data, the latter straightening the paths so that fewer integration steps suffice (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023). These models were scaled by moving to a latent space (Rombach et al., 2022), by transformer backbones (Peebles and Xie, 2023; Ma et al., 2024) and by larger, more efficient architectures (Podell et al., 2024; Esser et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2025a), with classifier-free guidance as a standard way to trade diversity for prompt fidelity (Ho and Salimans, 2021). Related generators include current text-to-image systems (OpenAI, 2022; Betker et al., 2023; Saharia et al., 2022; Black Forest Labs, 2024; Black Forest Labs, 2025; Team Seedream et al., 2025; Z-Image Team et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2025), multimodal models that both generate and understand images in one network (Chen et al., 2025b; Ma et al., 2025a; Xie et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2024b; OpenAI et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025a), trained on web-scale image–text data (Schuhmann et al., 2022; Zou, 2024), and video generators such as Wan and LongCat-Video (Team Wan et al., 2025; Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2025). These models typically learn the instantaneous velocity of the sampling flow, or an affine transformation of it such as the score or the predicted noise. Since this velocity is instantaneous, the sampler integrates it with many small steps, typically 32 or 64, which makes inference costly.

Few-step generation.

Sampling cost has been cut along several lines. Progressive distillation halves the number of steps repeatedly by training a student to match two teacher steps with one (Salimans and Ho, 2022). Consistency models map every point of a trajectory to its endpoint, and were extended to latent space, arbitrary trajectory jumps, multiple sub-intervals and segmented trajectories (Song et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2023a; Kim et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a; Ren et al., 2024); consistency has also been used as a training regulariser against sampling drift and to learn from noisy data (Daras et al., 2023; Daras et al., 2024). Shortcut models condition on the step size and learn to take large steps directly (Frans et al., 2025). Adversarial distillation adds a discriminator so that one to four steps produce sharp samples (Wang et al., 2023a; Sauer et al., 2025; Sauer et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2024; Chadebec et al., 2025; Lu and Song, 2025). Distribution matching distillation (DMD) trains the generator so that its output distribution matches the teacher’s, using the difference between a teacher score and the score of an auxiliary network fitted to the generator’s samples (Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a), an idea shared with Diff-Instruct and variational score distillation (Luo et al., 2023b; Wang et al., 2023b); later work scales it to flow models, splits it into sub-intervals, decouples guidance from matching, moves it to continuous time, regularises it with consistency, and adapts it to video (Ge et al., 2026a; Fan et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026b; Zheng et al., 2026b; Ge et al., 2026b; Nie et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2025). Flow maps learn the transport between any two noise levels. MeanFlow parameterises the average velocity over an interval and trains it through its identity with the instantaneous velocity (Geng et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026; Geng et al., 2026), and AnyFlow distils such a map on policy for any step count (Gu et al., 2026). Unlike the many-step generators above, these flow-map models learn an average velocity over an interval, which can be read as the direction of a secant of the sampling trajectory, differing substantially from the instantaneous velocity where the trajectory is curved.

Reinforcement learning for diffusion models.

RL fine-tuning of generators builds on policy optimisation (Levine, 2018; Schulman et al., 2017), preference optimisation (Rafailov et al., 2023) and group-relative advantages, which normalise rewards within a group of samples for the same prompt (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). For diffusion models, early work fine-tunes on human feedback (Lee et al., 2023), treats denoising as a Markov decision process optimised by policy gradients (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023), or optimises pairwise preferences directly (Wallace et al., 2024). FlowGRPO brings group-relative policy optimisation to flow models by turning the ODE sampler into an SDE with tractable transition likelihoods (Liu et al., 2025a); follow-ups extend it to video, mix ODE and SDE steps, weight timesteps, and preserve the noise coefficients of the sampler (Xue et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026a; He et al., 2026; Wang and Yu, 2025). A second family avoids transition likelihoods by acting on the forward process: AWM weights the pretraining loss by the advantage (Xue et al., 2026), reward-weighted and policy-gradient flow matching reweight or rescale the velocity regression (Fan et al., 2025; McAllister et al., 2026), adjoint matching is scaled to RL post-training (Bergmeister et al., 2026), and DiffusionNFT contrasts positive and negative implicit policies built from the model and the frozen policy that generated its rollouts (Zheng et al., 2026a), following NFT in language models (Chen et al., 2026b). A third family backpropagates differentiable rewards through the sampler, as in DRaFT and ReFL (Clark et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026); the recently proposed DiffusionOPSD (Zhou et al., 2026) belongs to this family but constructs detached points with normalised reward-gradient steps and fits the policy to them, thereby forming a surrogate gradient. These methods are built for an instantaneous velocity, and most of them need on-policy rollouts at every iteration, which are expensive with the many-step samplers discussed above; how to apply RL to few-step models is therefore an important question.

RL for few-step generators.

Closest to this paper are methods that fine-tune few-step models with rewards. Several combine DMD with RL, by adding a reward term to distillation, guiding distillation with reward gradients, or recasting distribution matching itself as a reward (Chen et al., 2026a; Jiang et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026a); others tune distilled models with non-differentiable rewards, Kullback–Leibler (KL) regularised alignment or pairwise sample optimisation (Luo et al., 2026; Luo, 2025; Miao et al., 2025). For flow maps, Flow-Map GRPO composes stochastic steps of a flow-map generator (Li et al., 2026b), MeanFlowNFT applies DiffusionNFT to an average-velocity model through its self-induced instantaneous field (Huang et al., 2026b), and RTDMD optimises a reward-tilted distribution matching objective (Huang et al., 2026a). These works mostly adapt one objective to one kind of few-step model; we instead give a common construction that extends FlowGRPO, AWM, DiffusionNFT, DiffusionOPSD and ReFL to average-velocity models, and compare them under one implementation.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Few-step Diffusion Models with On-Policy Distillation

We write t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] for the noise level, with data at t=0t=0 and Gaussian noise at t=1t=1. A plain xtx_{t} denotes a point at level tt on a sampling trajectory, and x~t\tilde{x}_{t} denotes a renoised state at level tt obtained by adding fresh noise to a clean sample (Equation (2)); every map below applies to either. The setting we focus on throughout is distillation, where a pretrained instantaneous-velocity field vreal​(x~t,t)v_{\mathrm{real}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t) is available and frozen, which we call the teacher, and the student uθ​(x~t,t,r)u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r) must reproduce its transport in one or a few network calls. The teacher is an ordinary flow-matching model, trained by regressing onto the conditional velocity vcond=ϵ−xv_{\mathrm{cond}}=\epsilon-x of a clean sample xx and Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), and it provides the student’s regression target in Equation (8) (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023). The student is the average-velocity generator (Geng et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026),

uθ​(xt,t,r)=1t−r​∫rtvθ​(xν,ν)​𝑑ν,u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,r)\;=\;\frac{1}{t-r}\int_{r}^{t}v_{\theta}(x_{\nu},\nu)\,\mathrm{d}\nu, (1)

where vθv_{\theta} is the instantaneous velocity induced by the student, xνx_{\nu} is the state at level ν\nu on the probability-flow trajectory of vθv_{\theta} through xtx_{t}, and uθ​(xt,t,t):=vθ​(xt,t)u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,t):=v_{\theta}(x_{t},t) closes the definition at r=tr=t. Throughout, we identify this induced field with the flow-matching marginal velocity of the student’s sample distribution pθp_{\theta}, vθ​(xt,t)=𝔼⁡[ϵ−x^∣xt]v_{\theta}(x_{t},t)=\mathbb{E}[\epsilon-\hat{x}\mid x_{t}] with x^∼pθ\hat{x}\sim p_{\theta} (Appendix A); the two coincide when the flow map is exact.

Unlike off-policy methods, which query the model at x~t=AddNoise​(x0,t)\tilde{x}_{t}=\textsc{AddNoise}(x_{0},t) with x0∼pdatax_{0}\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}, on-policy training draws the noised state from the student’s own distribution:

x~t=AddNoise​(x^θ,t)=(1−t)​x^θ+t​ϵ,x^θ∼pθ​(x),ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I).\tilde{x}_{t}=\textsc{AddNoise}\big(\hat{x}_{\theta},t\big)=(1-t)\,\hat{x}_{\theta}+t\,\epsilon,\qquad\hat{x}_{\theta}\sim p_{\theta}(x),\quad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (2)

The subscript θ\theta in Equation (2) is kept only where the sampler is differentiated. The samples x^θ\hat{x}_{\theta} are produced by a rollout operator Rollout, an ODE or SDE solver that maps Gaussian noise at level 11 to a clean sample at level 00 for a text prompt cc in MstepM_{\mathrm{step}} steps, on a grid 1=t0>t1>⋯>tMstep=01=t_{0}>t_{1}>\dots>t_{M_{\mathrm{step}}}=0:

x^θ=Rollout​(ϵ,uθ,c),x^θ,t0=ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I).\hat{x}_{\theta}=\textsc{Rollout}\big(\epsilon,\,u_{\theta},\,c\big),\qquad\hat{x}_{\theta,t_{0}}=\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (3)

For an instantaneous field, one Euler step of the solver between tjt_{j} and tj+1t_{j+1} is

x^θ,tj+1=x^θ,tj−(tj−tj+1)​vθ​(x^θ,tj,tj),\hat{x}_{\theta,t_{j+1}}=\hat{x}_{\theta,t_{j}}-(t_{j}-t_{j+1})\,v_{\theta}\big(\hat{x}_{\theta,t_{j}},t_{j}\big), (4)

which is only first-order accurate, so MstepM_{\mathrm{step}} must be large. A displacement is the time integral of the velocity, and by Equation (1) (t−r)​uθ(t-r)\,u_{\theta} equals this integral over [r,t][r,t]. With uθu_{\theta} as the generator, the Euler step is replaced by an exact jump,

x^θ,r=x^θ,t−(t−r)​uθ​(x^θ,t,t,r),\hat{x}_{\theta,r}=\hat{x}_{\theta,t}-(t-r)\,u_{\theta}\big(\hat{x}_{\theta,t},t,r\big), (5)

so a few-step sampler is a chain of MstepM_{\mathrm{step}} such jumps, each a single subtraction rather than an integration. Taking the whole interval at once, Mstep=1M_{\mathrm{step}}=1, t=1t=1 and r=0r=0, recovers the one-call generator.

MeanFlow.

According to the definition of uθu_{\theta} in Equation (1) (Geng et al., 2025), multiplying by (t−r)(t-r) and differentiating in tt eliminates the integral and leaves the MeanFlow identity

uθ​(x~t,t,r)=vθ​(x~t,t)−(t−r)​∂tuθ​(x~t,t,r),u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)\;=\;v_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t)\;-\;(t-r)\,\partial_{t}u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r), (6)

where ∂tuθ=d​uθ/d​t\partial_{t}u_{\theta}=\mathrm{d}u_{\theta}/\mathrm{d}t is the total derivative along the trajectory xνx_{\nu} of Equation (1); the implementation estimates it by a directional-difference estimate (Equation (87)). The identity follows from the definition Equation (1) and imposes no additional constraint; it expresses the average velocity as the instantaneous velocity minus (t−r)(t-r) times the total derivative of the average velocity with respect to tt.

Every use of Equation (6) treats this correction as detached, so we define it once with the stop-gradient sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot), which is the identity in the forward pass and zero in the backward pass,

J⁡[u,t,r]:=(t−r)​sg⁡(∂tu),J\big[u,\,t,\,r\big]\;:=\;(t-r)\,\operatorname{sg}\big(\partial_{t}u\big), (7)

the detached Jacobian-vector term. It gives the gap between an average velocity over [r,t][r,t] and the instantaneous one at tt, measured on the network itself and frozen before it is used. Substituting the teacher for vθv_{\theta} in Equation (6) then turns the identity into a regression whose target is assembled entirely from quantities available at the current state,

ℒMF=𝔼x~t,t,r​[‖uθ​(x~t,t,r)−(vreal​(x~t,t)−J⁡[uθ,t,r])‖2],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MF}}=\mathbb{E}_{\,\tilde{x}_{t},\,t,\,r}\Big[\left\lVert u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)-\big(v_{\mathrm{real}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t)-J\big[u_{\theta},\,t,\,r\big]\big)\right\rVert^{2}\Big], (8)

in which vrealv_{\mathrm{real}} is frozen and JJ contains a stop-gradient, so uθu_{\theta} is the only differentiated quantity. Setting r=tr=t recovers instantaneous-velocity distillation onto vrealv_{\mathrm{real}}; the case r<tr<t trains the flow map and hence the one-step transport x~θ,r=x~t−(t−r)​uθ​(x~t,t,r)\tilde{x}_{\theta,r}=\tilde{x}_{t}-(t-r)\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r) to level rr.

DMD.

Distribution matching distillation (Yin et al., 2024b; Yin et al., 2024a) does not regress uθu_{\theta} onto a target. It maintains a second, auxiliary velocity vϕ​(x~t,t)v_{\phi}(\tilde{x}_{t},t) with its own parameters ϕ\phi, fitted online by flow matching to the samples generated by the student. Its target is the conditional velocity of each sample instead of the teacher, because vϕv_{\phi} is meant to approximate the velocity of pθp_{\theta} instead of pdatap_{\mathrm{data}}:

ℒaux=𝔼x^∼pθ,ϵ,t​[‖vϕ​(x~t,t)−vcond‖2],x~t=AddNoise​(x^,t),vcond=ϵ−x^.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}}=\mathbb{E}_{\,\hat{x}\sim p_{\theta},\ \epsilon,\ t}\Big[\left\lVert v_{\phi}(\tilde{x}_{t},t)-v_{\mathrm{cond}}\right\rVert^{2}\Big],\qquad\tilde{x}_{t}=\textsc{AddNoise}(\hat{x},t),\quad v_{\mathrm{cond}}=\epsilon-\hat{x}. (9)

The difference between the two fields then gives the score difference in the gradient of the reverse KL divergence, which is used to train uθ​(x~t,t,r)u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r):

∇θℒDMD=𝔼ϵ,t∈(0,1)​[1−tt​sg⁡[vreal​(x~t,t)−vϕ​(x~t,t)]⊤​∂x^θ∂θ],\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DMD}}=\mathbb{E}_{\,\epsilon,\,t\in(0,1)}\Big[\frac{1-t}{t}\,\operatorname{sg}\big[v_{\mathrm{real}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t)-v_{\phi}(\tilde{x}_{t},t)\big]^{\!\top}\frac{\partial\,\hat{x}_{\theta}}{\partial\theta}\Big], (10)

The order of the two fields is fixed by the conversion between them. The score of the linear path is ∇logpt(x~t)=−𝔼[ϵ∣x~t]/t\nabla\log p_{t}(\tilde{x}_{t})=-\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid\tilde{x}_{t}]/t with 𝔼⁡[ϵ∣x~t]=x~t+(1−t)​v\mathbb{E}[\epsilon\mid\tilde{x}_{t}]=\tilde{x}_{t}+(1-t)v, so the difference ∇log⁡ptϕ−∇log⁡ptreal\nabla\log p^{\phi}_{t}-\nabla\log p^{\mathrm{real}}_{t} of the scores of the two fields, which the reverse KL produces, equals 1−tt​(vreal−vϕ)\frac{1-t}{t}\,(v_{\mathrm{real}}-v_{\phi}). Converting scores to velocities reverses the order of the two fields and introduces the score-to-velocity factor 1−tt\frac{1-t}{t}, which is positive on (0,1)(0,1) and is absorbed into a per-tt weight in practice. Descending Equation (10) therefore applies the direction +(vϕ−vreal)+(v_{\phi}-v_{\mathrm{real}}), reducing the mismatch to the data field relative to the auxiliary field that tracks pθp_{\theta}.

The term ∂x^θ/∂θ\partial\hat{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta requires a differentiable sampler, and the sampler used in practice is stochastic. A step at level tt does not move directly to the next level; it first maps the state to r=0r=0 with one network evaluation and then renoises the result to an intermediate level t′t^{\prime} with 0<t′<t0<t^{\prime}<t:

x^θ,0=x^θ,t−t​uθ​(x^θ,t,t,0),x^θ,t′=(1−t′)​x^θ,0+t′​ϵ′,ϵ′∼𝒩⁡(0,I).\hat{x}_{\theta,0}=\hat{x}_{\theta,t}-t\,u_{\theta}\big(\hat{x}_{\theta,t},t,0\big),\qquad\hat{x}_{\theta,t^{\prime}}=(1-t^{\prime})\,\hat{x}_{\theta,0}+t^{\prime}\,\epsilon^{\prime},\qquad\epsilon^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). (11)

Unlike the deterministic chain Equation (5), this sampler draws fresh noise ϵ′\epsilon^{\prime} at every step, so the state at level t′t^{\prime} is not a deterministic function of the previous state.

The levels follow a fixed grid of Mstep+1M_{\mathrm{step}}+1 values spanning MstepM_{\mathrm{step}} intervals; a step count ℓ∈{1,…,Mstep}\ell\in\{1,\dots,M_{\mathrm{step}}\} is drawn per update, and only the last step remains in the computation graph, with all earlier steps detached. The backward pass therefore requires one network evaluation for any ℓ\ell. Moreover, the differentiated evaluation is uθ​(⋅,t,0)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,0) at the level that the grid assigns to step ℓ\ell, so randomising ℓ\ell changes this level across updates. Over training, the gradient therefore reaches uθ​(⋅,t,0)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,0) at every grid level tt instead of a single one.

3.2 Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Models

FlowGRPO.

FlowGRPO combines a GRPO-style group baseline with a PPO transition objective (Schulman et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a). It scores a group of KK rollouts that share a prompt cc, and turns the raw scores into a group-normalised advantage. Writing R(i)=R⁡(𝒟⁡(x^(i)),c)R^{(i)}=R\big(\mathcal{D}(\hat{x}^{(i)}),c\big) for the endpoint reward of member ii (𝒟\mathcal{D} the decoder), the advantage standardises the reward within the group,

A(i)=R(i)−mean⁡({R})std⁡({R})+εstd,i=1,…,K.A^{(i)}=\frac{R^{(i)}-\operatorname{mean}\big(\{R\}\big)}{\operatorname{std}\big(\{R\}\big)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{std}}},\qquad i=1,\dots,K. (12)

Here {R}\{R\} denotes the KK rewards of the group and εstd>0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{std}}>0 is a small floor. The advantage is a detached per-sample scalar with zero mean across the group; no value network is fitted, and the group mean serves as the baseline. AWM below uses the same A(i)A^{(i)}; DiffusionNFT uses a bounded transform of it.

FlowGRPO formulates the stochastic differential equation (SDE) sampler as a Markov decision process, whose state is the current noisy sample xtx_{t} (a point on the sampling trajectory, in the convention of §3) together with the prompt and the level and whose action is the next state produced by the sampler; the Gaussian transition pθtr​(xr∣xt)p^{\mathrm{tr}}_{\theta}(x_{r}\mid x_{t}) then provides a likelihood, which the deterministic sampler lacks. Optimisation is proximal policy optimisation on the realised action xrx_{r},

ℒGRPO=−𝔼i,t​[min⁡{A(i)​ρtr(i),A(i)​clip⁡(ρtr(i),1±εclip)}],ρtr=pθtr​(xr∣xt)poldtr​(xr∣xt).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}=-\,\mathbb{E}_{\,i,\,t}\Big[\min\big\{A^{(i)}\rho_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i)},\;A^{(i)}\operatorname{clip}\big(\rho_{\mathrm{tr}}^{(i)},1\pm\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}\big)\big\}\Big],\qquad\rho_{\mathrm{tr}}=\frac{p^{\mathrm{tr}}_{\theta}(x_{r}\mid x_{t})}{p^{\mathrm{tr}}_{\mathrm{old}}(x_{r}\mid x_{t})}. (13)

Here the old policy is the frozen policy, with parameters θold\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, that generated the rollouts on which the current policy is trained; it receives no gradient. In our implementation, θold\theta_{\mathrm{old}} is an exponential moving average (EMA) of θ\theta, refreshed after every outer iteration (§5.1) with the EMA-decay ratio as the weight kept on the previous θold\theta_{\mathrm{old}}; an EMA-decay ratio of 0.00.0 therefore copies θ\theta, so that θold=θ\theta_{\mathrm{old}}=\theta at the start of every outer iteration. The subscript old\mathrm{old} marks its quantities, so poldtrp^{\mathrm{tr}}_{\mathrm{old}} is its transition density, voldv_{\mathrm{old}} its instantaneous velocity and poldp_{\mathrm{old}} the distribution of its rollouts. The clipping radius is εclip\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}. For later clipped surrogates, define the detached unclipped-gradient gate

χ⁡(z,A):=[(A>0∧z≤1+εclip)∨(A<0∧z≥1−εclip)],χ⁡(z,0):=0.\chi(z,A):=\mathbf{1}\!\left[(A>0\ \wedge\ z\leq 1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}})\ \vee\ (A<0\ \wedge\ z\geq 1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}})\right],\qquad\chi(z,0):=0. (14)

At the two clipping kinks this convention selects the derivative of the unclipped branch. The sign of the reward advantage determines the direction of the update of the mean μθ\mu_{\theta} of the Gaussian transition (the scoring kernel defined in Equation (95)) relative to the visited noisy state xrx_{r}.

AWM.

Advantage Weighted Matching (Xue et al., 2026) keeps the signed advantage but does not evaluate a likelihood on the reverse process. Each update draws a fresh (t,ϵ)(t,\epsilon) and constructs both the noised state and the regression target from the rollout sample,

x~t(i)=AddNoise​(x^(i),t)=(1−t)​x^(i)+t​ϵ,vcond(i)=ϵ−x^(i),\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)}=\textsc{AddNoise}\big(\hat{x}^{(i)},t\big)=(1-t)\,\hat{x}^{(i)}+t\,\epsilon,\qquad v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)}=\epsilon-\hat{x}^{(i)}, (15)

where vcond(i)v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)} is the conditional velocity, i.e., the velocity of the straight path from x^(i)\hat{x}^{(i)} to ϵ\epsilon, which is computed from the two endpoints without a network evaluation. AWM then observes that the flow-matching loss against that target is, for a suitable time weight w⁡(t)w(t), an evidence-lower-bound surrogate for the sequence-level log-likelihood of the clean sample,

log⁡pθ​(x^(i)∣c)≥log⁡p^θ​(x^(i)∣c)+const,log⁡p^θ​(x^(i)∣c):=−𝔼t,ϵ​[w⁡(t)​‖vθ​(x~t(i),t)−vcond(i)‖2],\log p_{\theta}\big(\hat{x}^{(i)}\mid c\big)\;\geq\;\log\hat{p}_{\theta}\big(\hat{x}^{(i)}\mid c\big)+\mathrm{const},\qquad\log\hat{p}_{\theta}\big(\hat{x}^{(i)}\mid c\big):=-\,\mathbb{E}_{\,t,\,\epsilon}\Big[w(t)\,\left\lVert v_{\theta}\big(\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},t\big)-v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)}\right\rVert^{2}\Big], (16)

so that the policy-gradient term A(i)​∇θ​log⁡p^θA^{(i)}\nabla_{\theta}\log\hat{p}_{\theta} reduces to the pretraining objective reweighted per sample:

ℒAWM=𝔼i,t,ϵ​[A(i)​w​(t)​‖vθ​(x~t(i),t)−vcond(i)‖2],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AWM}}=\mathbb{E}_{\,i,\,t,\,\epsilon}\Big[A^{(i)}\,w(t)\,\left\lVert v_{\theta}\big(\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},t\big)-v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)}\right\rVert^{2}\Big], (17)

with the time weight w⁡(t)=1w(t)=1 in the original AWM (our implementation effectively uses w⁡(t)=τAWM2w(t)=\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}^{2}, §5.4) and a velocity-space proximal penalty ‖vθ−vold‖2\left\lVert v_{\theta}-v_{\mathrm{old}}\right\rVert^{2} against the old policy voldv_{\mathrm{old}}, called a KL term in AWM, added for stability. Minimising Equation (17) decreases the matching residual at x^(i)\hat{x}^{(i)} when A(i)>0A^{(i)}>0 and increases it when A(i)<0A^{(i)}<0. Since no reverse-time discretisation appears, the sampler can be chosen freely.

DiffusionNFT.

Negative-aware fine-tuning (Zheng et al., 2026a) builds on an optimality-variable construction (Levine, 2018) and requires neither a likelihood nor a signed weight. It first maps the advantage to a bounded optimality probability with a normaliser Zc=std⁡({R})+εstdZ_{c}=\operatorname{std}(\{R\})+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{std}},

r^(i)=12+12​clip⁡[R(i)−mean⁡({R})Zc,−1, 1]=12+12​clip⁡(A(i),−1, 1)∈[0,1],\hat{r}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{clip}\!\left[\frac{R^{(i)}-\operatorname{mean}\big(\{R\}\big)}{Z_{c}},\;-1,\;1\right]=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{clip}\big(A^{(i)},\,-1,\,1\big)\;\in[0,1], (18)

since the bracketed quotient then equals Equation (12). Thus A(i)A^{(i)} is signed, unclipped and zero-mean under Equation (12) and enters as a multiplier, whereas r^(i)\hat{r}^{(i)} is bounded, monotone in A(i)A^{(i)} and equal to 12\tfrac{1}{2} when A(i)=0A^{(i)}=0, and enters as a mixing weight. A positive advantage gives r^(i)>12\hat{r}^{(i)}>\tfrac{1}{2} and hence a larger weight on the positive branch.

Each update then draws a fresh (t,ϵ)(t,\epsilon) and forms the noised state x~t(i)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)} and the conditional velocity vcond(i)v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)} as in Equation (15); the target is the same as in AWM, and, besides the weight, only the regressed quantity differs. Two implicit policies are built from one trainable network vθv_{\theta} and the frozen old policy voldv_{\mathrm{old}}, both evaluated at that same x~t(i)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)} and mixed by a branch coefficient β\beta:

vθ±​(x~t(i),t):=(1∓β)​vold​(x~t(i),t)±β​vθ​(x~t(i),t).v^{\pm}_{\theta}\big(\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},t\big):=(1\mp\beta)\,v_{\mathrm{old}}\big(\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},t\big)\pm\beta\,v_{\theta}\big(\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},t\big). (19)

Both are regressed onto the same target vcond(i)v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)}, mixed by r^(i)\hat{r}^{(i)}:

ℒNFT=𝔼i,t,ϵ​[r^(i)​‖vθ+−vcond(i)‖2+(1−r^(i))​‖vθ−−vcond(i)‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NFT}}=\mathbb{E}_{\,i,\,t,\,\epsilon}\Big[\hat{r}^{(i)}\,\left\lVert v^{+}_{\theta}-v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)}\right\rVert^{2}+\big(1-\hat{r}^{(i)}\big)\,\left\lVert v^{-}_{\theta}-v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)}\right\rVert^{2}\Big]. (20)

Both branches are affine in the same trainable network vθv_{\theta}; since voldv_{\mathrm{old}}, vcond(i)v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)} and r^(i)\hat{r}^{(i)} are detached, vθv_{\theta} is the only differentiated quantity in Equation (20).

4 Framework

Each RL method of §3.2 increases the relative probability of high-reward samples under the rollout distribution poldp_{\mathrm{old}} of the old policy. The methods differ in the space in which the update is formulated (transition densities, velocities, or rewards differentiated through the sample) and in how a few-step network computes the quantities that the update requires. This section resolves both differences in three steps, summarised in Figure 2.

  1. (i)

    Transformation to xx-space (§4.1, Figure 2a). Under the linear noise schedule a velocity transports a state affinely, so each objective of §3 can be expressed through a common prediction in xx-space. By default this prediction is the policy prediction x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta}; MeanFlow and FewStepGRPO keep an explicitly marked level-rr quantity. In xx-space the methods become directly comparable.

  2. (ii)

    Decomposition of the gradient (§4.2, Figure 2b). In xx-space, the gradient of each of these losses is the transposed Jacobian (∂x~θ/∂θ)⊤(\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta)^{\top} applied to the sum of a reward-free self-regression toward an anchor x~reg\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}, which limits how far the prediction moves, and a reward augmentation along x~rwd−x~base\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}, which contains the reward. A method is then specified by the prediction, three anchors (x~reg,x~rwd,x~base)(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}},\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}},\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}) and three weights (Wreg,Wrwd,ω)(W_{\mathrm{reg}},W_{\mathrm{rwd}},\omega) instead of a new loss.

  3. (iii)

    Adaptation to few-step models (§4.3, Figure 2c). The framework requires instantaneous velocities, whereas a few-step model outputs an average velocity. Its anchors are therefore computed either at the end of the transport curve (u-form) or along the tangent at the current state (v-form). The latter recovers the instantaneous velocity from the network itself, as in MeanFlow, or from an auxiliary network, as in DMD.

§5 then specifies the predictions, anchors and weights of each family.

4.1 Transformation to x-space

The objectives of §3 are written in transition-density or velocity space. Under the linear noise schedule, a velocity instead identifies a point in xx-space at any chosen level rr. This xx-space includes noisy level-rr points; clean samples correspond to r=0r=0.

For any point xtx_{t} at level tt (in particular a renoised state x~t\tilde{x}_{t}), define the affine transport

X⁡[xt,v,r]:=xt−(t−r)​v.X\big[x_{t},\,v,\,r\big]\;:=\;x_{t}-(t-r)\,v. (21)

For two velocities evaluated at the same xtx_{t} and transported to the same level r<tr<t,

‖va−vb‖2=1(t−r)2​‖X⁡[xt,va,r]−X⁡[xt,vb,r]‖2.\left\lVert v_{a}-v_{b}\right\rVert^{2}\;=\;\frac{1}{(t-r)^{2}}\,\left\lVert X\big[x_{t},\,v_{a},\,r\big]-X\big[x_{t},\,v_{b},\,r\big]\right\rVert^{2}. (22)

Thus a velocity MSE equals a scaled MSE between transported points in xx-space. At the clean level r=0r=0 the factor is t−2t^{-2}, and we omit the level subscript. In particular, for x~t=(1−t)​x+t​ϵ\tilde{x}_{t}=(1-t)x+t\epsilon and vcond=ϵ−xv_{\mathrm{cond}}=\epsilon-x, Equation (21) gives X⁡[x~t,vcond, 0]=xX\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,v_{\mathrm{cond}},\,0\big]=x.

For the reward objectives below, a detached rollout endpoint x^(i)\hat{x}^{(i)} is re-noised to x~t(i)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)}, and the policy provides the current policy prediction

x~θ(i)=X⁡[x~t(i),vθ, 0]=x~t(i)−t​vθ,\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}\;=\;X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},\,v_{\theta},\,0\big]\;=\;\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)}-t\,v_{\theta}, (23)

while the conditional target maps back to x^(i)\hat{x}^{(i)}. Hence the loss compares predictions at the same state x~t(i)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)}, and only x~θ(i)\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)} is differentiated. §4.3 constructs this prediction when the network outputs an average velocity instead of an instantaneous one. Analysing a loss in xx-space therefore shows how the prediction x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} must change to reduce the loss, i.e., which points x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} moves toward and which it moves away from. The same map applied to the old policy gives the old policy’s prediction

x~old(i)=X⁡[x~t(i),vold, 0],\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},\,v_{\mathrm{old}},\,0\big], (24)

which serves as an anchor in several methods below; its few-step variants, the self-induced prediction of Example 5 and the u-prediction and JJ-free query of §4.3, are collected in Appendix A.

Example 1 (AWM in x-space).

The target of Equation (17) is vcond(i)v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)}, and Equation (21) sends it to the rollout endpoint itself, X⁡[x~t(i),vcond(i), 0]=x^(i)X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},\,v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)},\,0\big]=\hat{x}^{(i)}. Applying Equation (22),

ℒAWM=𝔼i,t,ϵ​[A(i)​w⁡(t)t2​‖x~θ(i)−x^(i)‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AWM}}=\mathbb{E}_{\,i,\,t,\,\epsilon}\Big[A^{(i)}\,\frac{w(t)}{t^{2}}\;\left\lVert\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\hat{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert^{2}\Big]. (25)

The method is a squared residual between the current prediction and the model’s sample, weighted by the signed advantage. Taking w⁡(t)=t2w(t)=t^{2} cancels the prefactor and gives an xx-space weight independent of tt; this is the choice our few-step implementation makes up to a floor (§5.4).

Example 2 (DiffusionNFT in x-space).

The target of Equation (20) is again vcond(i)v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)}, so Equation (21) sends it to the same rollout endpoint x^(i)\hat{x}^{(i)}. Only the prediction differs; the two implicit policies Equation (19) are mapped to

x~θ±=X⁡[x~t(i),vθ±, 0]=x~old(i)±β⁡(x~θ(i)−x~old(i)),\tilde{x}^{\pm}_{\theta}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},\,v^{\pm}_{\theta},\,0\big]=\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}\pm\beta\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}\big), (26)

with x~old(i)\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}} as in Equation (24). Applying Equation (22) to each branch,

ℒNFT=𝔼i,t,ϵ​[1t2​(r^(i)​‖x~θ+−x^(i)‖2+(1−r^(i))​‖x~θ−−x^(i)‖2)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NFT}}=\mathbb{E}_{\,i,\,t,\,\epsilon}\Big[\frac{1}{t^{2}}\Big(\hat{r}^{(i)}\,\left\lVert\tilde{x}^{+}_{\theta}-\hat{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert^{2}+\big(1-\hat{r}^{(i)}\big)\,\left\lVert\tilde{x}^{-}_{\theta}-\hat{x}^{(i)}\right\rVert^{2}\Big)\Big]. (27)

The method mixes two squared residuals to the model’s sample with weights r^(i)\hat{r}^{(i)} and 1−r^(i)1-\hat{r}^{(i)}. The positive branch receives more weight when the reward of the sample is above the group mean, and the negative branch when it is below. The common prefactor t−2t^{-2} can be absorbed into the weights, so the mixing itself is independent of tt.

4.2 The Decoupled Loss Decomposition

Under the transformation Equation (21), the gradient of each objective considered here is the transposed Jacobian (∂x~θ(i)/∂θ)⊤(\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}/\partial\theta)^{\top} applied to the sum of two vectors in xx-space (at the clean level by default and at level rr in the explicit exceptions). We adopt this form as the general framework,

∇θℒ(i)=2​(∂x~θ(i)∂θ)⊤​[Wreg(i)​(x~θ(i)−x~reg(i))⏟self-regression−Wrwd(i)​ω(i)​(x~rwd(i)−x~base(i))⏟reward augmentation],\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}^{(i)}=2\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\!\top}\Big[\;\underbrace{W_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}\big)}_{\text{self-regression}}\;-\;\underbrace{W_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}\;\omega^{(i)}\big(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}\big)}_{\text{reward augmentation}}\Big], (28)

with Wreg(i),Wrwd(i)≥0W_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)},W_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}\geq 0 and ω(i)∈ℝ\omega^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R} detached scalars. The factor 22 from differentiating a square is kept outside the bracket, so all weights below are defined relative to Equation (28); for example, the loss W​‖x~θ−x~rwd‖2W\left\lVert\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}\right\rVert^{2} corresponds to Wrwd=WW_{\mathrm{rwd}}=W. The prediction x~θ(i)\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)} is constructed by first noising the rollout sample x^(i)\hat{x}^{(i)} to level tt and then transporting the resulting state x~t(i)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)} back to r=0r=0 by Equation (21). Here ω(i)\omega^{(i)} is the signed reward coefficient used in the general loss Equation (30), and |ω(i)||\omega^{(i)}| is its magnitude. For methods whose coefficient follows the advantage, a non-zero ω(i)\omega^{(i)} has the sign of A(i)A^{(i)} in the theoretical weighting (the implemented DiffusionNFT weighting of §5.5 can deviate), and a clipping gate may set it to zero.

Self-regression.

The first term does not depend on the reward. It vanishes at x~θ(i)=x~reg(i)\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)} and grows with the distance from this anchor, so its gradient moves the prediction back toward the anchor. This self-regression term limits how far the reward-augmentation term can move the prediction and therefore helps protect against reward hacking.

The regression anchor is therefore chosen as a prediction that the policy should stay close to. A common choice is the old policy’s prediction x~old(i)=X⁡[x~t(i),vold, 0]\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old}}^{(i)}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},\,v_{\mathrm{old}},\,0\big], so that the term penalises the deviation of the current prediction from that of the policy used for sampling. Since x~θ(i)\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)} is computed from x~t(i)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)}, the anchor x~reg(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)} must be computed from the same x~t(i)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)}; otherwise, the difference x~θ(i)−x~reg(i)\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)} would mix a change of the velocity field with a change of the state and would no longer measure the deviation that the term is meant to bound.

Reward augmentation.

For fixed anchors, the second term contributes a vector that does not depend on the current prediction and contains the reward. Under gradient descent it moves x~θ(i)\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)} along +ω(i)​(x~rwd(i)−x~base(i))+\omega^{(i)}(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}), a displacement whose direction is set by the sign of ω(i)\omega^{(i)} and whose coefficient has magnitude |ω(i)||\omega^{(i)}|. The magnitude of the full term also depends on Wrwd(i)W_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)} and on the anchor displacement x~rwd(i)−x~base(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}.

The rewarded anchor x~rwd(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)} is usually the rollout sample, since transporting x~t(i)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)} with the conditional velocity gives X⁡[x~t(i),vcond(i), 0]=x^(i)X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},\,v_{\mathrm{cond}}^{(i)},\,0\big]=\hat{x}^{(i)}. This choice is natural because A(i)A^{(i)} is obtained by scoring x^(i)\hat{x}^{(i)} and provides no direct information about other points. For methods whose coefficient follows the advantage, the sign of ω(i)\omega^{(i)} determines whether the prediction moves toward x~rwd(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)} or away from it.

The other end, x~base(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}, is the baseline anchor. The displacement x~rwd(i)−x~base(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)} points from the baseline anchor to the rewarded anchor, so x~base(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)} sets the reference point and the line along which the reward acts. Admissible choices for x~base(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)} include the old policy’s prediction x~old(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old}}^{(i)} and the detached current prediction sg⁡(x~θ(i))\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}). In the RL methods, x~base(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)} is also evaluated at the state x~t(i)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)} from which x~θ(i)\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)} is computed, so that the two anchors define a displacement in the space on which the update acts.

An intuitive example.

Consider a group-advantage-based method with the group-mean advantage of Equation (12) and a group in which A(1)>A(2)>0>A(3)A^{(1)}>A^{(2)}>0>A^{(3)}. Members 11 and 22 both score above the group mean, so ω(1),ω(2)>0\omega^{(1)},\omega^{(2)}>0 and both predictions are attracted toward their rewarded samples. Member 22 is not penalised for scoring lower than member 11; it only receives a coefficient of smaller or equal magnitude, since |ω(1)|≥|ω(2)||\omega^{(1)}|\geq|\omega^{(2)}| in AWM and in the theoretical DiffusionNFT weighting below. Member 33 scores below the mean, so ω(3)<0\omega^{(3)}<0 and its prediction is repelled away from x~rwd(3)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(3)}, in the direction x~base(3)−x~rwd(3)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(3)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(3)}. Whether a prediction is attracted or repelled is therefore determined by the baseline-subtracted advantage A(i)A^{(i)} and not by the raw reward; a sample with a high reward is still repelled if it scores below its group mean.

Recovering the loss.

For any VθV_{\theta} and any detached UU,

−(∂Vθ∂θ)⊤​U=∇θ12​‖Vθ−sg⁡(Vθ+U)‖2.-\left(\frac{\partial V_{\theta}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\!\top}U\;=\;\nabla_{\theta}\,\tfrac{1}{2}\left\lVert V_{\theta}-\operatorname{sg}\big(V_{\theta}+U\big)\right\rVert^{2}. (29)

Therefore, applying Equation (29) with Vθ=x~θ(i)V_{\theta}=\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)} and U=g(i):=ω(i)​(x~rwd(i)−x~base(i))U=g^{(i)}:=\omega^{(i)}(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}) writes Equation (28) as a sum of two squares,

ℒ(i)=Wreg(i)​‖x~θ(i)−x~reg(i)‖2⏟ℒreg(i)+Wrwd(i)​‖x~θ(i)−sg⁡(x~θ(i)+g(i))‖2⏟ℒrwd(i),\mathcal{L}^{(i)}=\underbrace{W_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}\left\lVert\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}\right\rVert^{2}}_{\textstyle\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{reg}}}\;+\;\underbrace{W_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}\left\lVert\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\operatorname{sg}\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}+g^{(i)}\big)\right\rVert^{2}}_{\textstyle\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{rwd}}}, (30)

which is the form §5 implements.

Example 3 (Decoupling AWM loss).

Applying the same decomposition to Equation (25) gives a limiting case of Equation (28). Differentiating it and rewriting the residual as a difference of anchors,

∇θℒAWM(i)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{AWM}} =2​w⁡(t)t2​A(i)​(∂x~θ(i)∂θ)⊤​(x~θ(i)−x^(i))\displaystyle=2\,\frac{w(t)}{t^{2}}\,A^{(i)}\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\!\top}\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\hat{x}^{(i)}\big) (31)
=−2​(∂x~θ(i)∂θ)⊤​w⁡(t)t2​A(i)​(x^(i)−sg⁡(x~θ(i))),\displaystyle=-2\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\!\top}\frac{w(t)}{t^{2}}\,A^{(i)}\,\big(\hat{x}^{(i)}-\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)})\big),

which is Equation (28) with Wreg=0W_{\mathrm{reg}}=0:

Wreg(i)=0,x~rwd(i)=x^(i),x~base(i)=sg⁡(x~θ(i)),Wrwd(i)=w⁡(t)t2,ω(i)=A(i).W_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}=0,\qquad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}=\hat{x}^{(i)},\qquad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}=\operatorname{sg}\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}\big),\qquad W_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}=\frac{w(t)}{t^{2}},\qquad\omega^{(i)}=A^{(i)}. (32)

The anchor x~reg(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)} is arbitrary, since it is multiplied by zero. Compared with the DiffusionNFT decomposition (Example 4 below, Equation (35)), there are three main differences. First, the baseline anchor is the detached current prediction, so one end of the reward displacement is fixed and the other moves with the policy. The term is therefore recomputed at every step and is proportional to the residual x^(i)−sg⁡(x~θ(i))\hat{x}^{(i)}-\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}) instead of being a fixed displacement; this is why AWM can be written as the single weighted square Equation (25). Second, in Equation (32) the magnitude |ω(i)|=|A(i)||\omega^{(i)}|=|A^{(i)}| is not clipped, whereas in DiffusionNFT it saturates at 1/β1/\beta. Third, with Wreg(i)=0W_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}=0 the matching loss contains no self-regression term; this role is played by the additional velocity-space proximal penalty ‖vθ−vold‖2\left\lVert v_{\theta}-v_{\mathrm{old}}\right\rVert^{2} of §3.2, which under Equation (22) is a self-regression toward the old policy’s prediction x~old(i)\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}.

Example 4 (Decoupling DiffusionNFT loss).

Applying the same decomposition to Equation (27) yields both terms of Equation (28). The two branches Equation (26) are affine in the same current prediction, so

∂x~θ+∂θ=β​∂x~θ(i)∂θ,∂x~θ−∂θ=−β​∂x~θ(i)∂θ.\frac{\partial\tilde{x}^{+}_{\theta}}{\partial\theta}=\beta\,\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}}{\partial\theta},\qquad\frac{\partial\tilde{x}^{-}_{\theta}}{\partial\theta}=-\beta\,\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}}{\partial\theta}. (33)

Differentiating Equation (27) and writing x~base(i):=x~old(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}:=\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}, the two branches collapse onto a single Jacobian. Since r^(i)=12+12​clip⁡(A(i),−1,1)\hat{r}^{(i)}=\tfrac{1}{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{clip}(A^{(i)},-1,1),

∇θℒNFT(i)=2​β2t2​(∂x~θ(i)∂θ)⊤​[(x~θ(i)−x~base(i))−clip⁡(A(i),−1,1)β​(x^(i)−x~base(i))],\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{NFT}}=\frac{2\beta^{2}}{t^{2}}\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\!\top}\Big[\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}\big)-\frac{\operatorname{clip}\big(A^{(i)},-1,1\big)}{\beta}\big(\hat{x}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}\big)\Big], (34)

which matches Equation (28) term by term, with a self-regression toward x~base(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)} and a reward augmentation along the fixed direction x^(i)−x~base(i)\hat{x}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}. The corresponding anchors and weights are

x~reg(i)=x~base(i)=X⁡[x~t(i),vold, 0],x~rwd(i)=x^(i),Wreg(i)=Wrwd(i)=β2t2,ω(i)=clip⁡(A(i),−1,1)β.\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},\,v_{\mathrm{old}},\,0\big],\quad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}=\hat{x}^{(i)},\quad W_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}^{(i)}=\frac{\beta^{2}}{t^{2}},\quad\omega^{(i)}=\frac{\operatorname{clip}\big(A^{(i)},-1,1\big)}{\beta}. (35)

Both anchors coincide at the old policy’s clean prediction, so DiffusionNFT regularises toward the point from which it measures the reward. The rewarded sample is the rollout produced by the model. The two weights are equal, which allows the published loss to be written as one fused square up to a detached term. The signed reward coefficient ω(i)=clip⁡(A(i),−1,1)/β\omega^{(i)}=\operatorname{clip}(A^{(i)},-1,1)/\beta has a magnitude that increases with |A(i)||A^{(i)}| and saturates at 1/β1/\beta because of the clip. In comparison, methods with Wreg(i)=0W_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}=0, such as AWM above, drop the self-regression from the matching loss.

Example 5 (Reward Augmentation for DMD and MeanFlow).

The decomposition also applies to reward-free distillation losses and yields their decoupled form. Neither objective scores a group, so there is no advantage and no index (i)(i); both move the policy toward the teacher. In the decomposition this is the limiting case

ω≡1,\omega\equiv 1,

i.e., a unit positive coefficient for every sample, with the rewarded anchor set to the teacher’s prediction

x~real=X⁡[x~t,vreal, 0]=x~t−t​vreal.\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,v_{\mathrm{real}},\,0\big]=\tilde{x}_{t}-tv_{\mathrm{real}}. (36)

MeanFlow. The network output in Equation (8) is an average velocity, so the corresponding instantaneous velocity is recovered before Equation (21) is applied. Rearranging the MeanFlow identity Equation (6) with Equation (7) recovers it as uθ+J⁡[uθ,t,r]u_{\theta}+J\big[u_{\theta},\,t,\,r\big]. The correction JJ is detached, so we evaluate it, together with the average velocity it corrects, on the frozen copy uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} of the network, which is sg⁡(uθ)\operatorname{sg}(u_{\theta}) in distillation and the old policy in RL. In particular, in MeanFlow uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} equals uθu_{\theta} in value; we write uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} only to unify the notation with the RL methods below:

vind​(x~t,t,r):=uold​(x~t,t,r)+J⁡[uold,t,r],v_{\mathrm{ind}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)\;:=\;u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big], (37)

and we call vindv_{\mathrm{ind}} the self-induced instantaneous velocity. It is computed from the average velocity and its total derivative with respect to tt, without a second network, and coincides with the instantaneous velocity of uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} wherever the flow map is exact. Its clean prediction is

x~ind=X⁡[x~t,vind, 0]=x~t−t​vind,\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,v_{\mathrm{ind}},\,0\big]=\tilde{x}_{t}-t\,v_{\mathrm{ind}}, (38)

where the subscript indicates the velocity used. Both vindv_{\mathrm{ind}} and x~ind\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}} are detached.

Both fields are now instantaneous, so Equation (21) transports them over the same interval. According to Equation (8), the prediction in xx-space is extended from the clean level to any level r<tr<t. Transporting with the teacher and with the self-induced velocity to level rr,

x~real,r=X⁡[x~t,vreal,r]=x~t+(r−t)​vreal,x~ind,r=X⁡[x~t,vind,r]=x~t+(r−t)​vind,\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real},r}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,v_{\mathrm{real}},\,r\big]=\tilde{x}_{t}+(r-t)\,v_{\mathrm{real}},\qquad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind},r}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,v_{\mathrm{ind}},\,r\big]=\tilde{x}_{t}+(r-t)\,v_{\mathrm{ind}}, (39)

whose clean ends at r=0r=0 are Equation (36) and Equation (38). The policy’s own transport with the same detached J=J⁡[uold,t,r]J=J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big] is X⁡[x~t,uθ+J,r]=x~θ,r+(r−t)​JX\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J,\,r\big]=\tilde{x}_{\theta,r}+(r-t)J, with x~θ,r=X⁡[x~t,uθ,r]\tilde{x}_{\theta,r}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta},\,r\big], and equals x~ind,r\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind},r} in value. For r<tr<t, Equation (8) is

ℒMF=𝔼x~t,t,r​[‖X⁡[x~t,uθ+J,r]−x~real,r‖2(t−r)2],r<t.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MF}}=\mathbb{E}_{\,\tilde{x}_{t},\,t,\,r}\!\left[\frac{\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J,\,r\big]-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real},r}\right\rVert^{2}}{(t-r)^{2}}\right],\qquad r<t. (40)

At r=tr=t the quotient is defined by continuity:

limr↑t‖X⁡[x~t,uθ+J,r]−x~real,r‖2(t−r)2=‖uθ​(x~t,t,t)−vreal​(x~t,t)‖2.\lim_{r\uparrow t}\frac{\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J,\,r\big]-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real},r}\right\rVert^{2}}{(t-r)^{2}}=\left\lVert u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,t)-v_{\mathrm{real}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t)\right\rVert^{2}.

Thus MeanFlow is the squared velocity residual written as a scaled distance between level-rr predictions. To obtain the loss form from Equation (28), we differentiate the average velocity, since JJ is detached:

∂∂θ​X​[x~t,uθ+J,r]=∂∂θ​[x~t+(r−t)​(uθ+J⁡[uold,t,r])]=∂x~θ,r∂θ,\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J,\,r\big]=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Big[\tilde{x}_{t}+(r-t)\big(u_{\theta}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big]\big)\Big]=\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta,r}}{\partial\theta}, (41)

where x~θ,r\tilde{x}_{\theta,r} is the one-step transport Equation (5) used by the sampler. Since JJ is detached, it shifts the prediction without changing its Jacobian. For r<tr<t, the gradient therefore corresponds to the reward augmentation,

∇θℒMF=− 2​(∂x~θ,r∂θ)⊤​1(t−r)2​(x~real,r−x~ind,r),\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MF}}=-\,2\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta,r}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\top}\frac{1}{(t-r)^{2}}\,\big(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real},r}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind},r}\big), (42)

which is the second term of Equation (28), as

Wreg=0,x~rwd=x~real,r,x~base=x~ind,r,Wrwd=1(t−r)2,ω=1.W_{\mathrm{reg}}=0,\quad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real},r},\quad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind},r},\quad W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\frac{1}{(t-r)^{2}},\quad\omega=1. (43)

These xx-space definitions apply for r<tr<t. At r=tr=t we use the velocity-space limit above; no finite value of Wrwd=(t−r)−2W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=(t-r)^{-2} is assigned to this case. Here the Jacobian is ∂x~θ,r/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta,r}/\partial\theta instead of ∂x~θ/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta, because the reward augmentation acts at level rr, which is resampled at every update.

DMD. The DMD gradient Equation (10) contains a velocity difference, and Equation (21) converts it into a difference of clean predictions. With x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} in place of the sampler output x^θ\hat{x}_{\theta}, the reverse KL of DMD evaluates the two fields at the noised prediction x~t′=AddNoise​(sg⁡(x~θ),t)\tilde{x}_{t}^{\prime}=\textsc{AddNoise}\big(\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}),t\big) rather than at x~t\tilde{x}_{t}; we write x~real=X⁡[x~t′,vreal, 0]\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{\prime},\,v_{\mathrm{real}},\,0\big] and x~aux=X⁡[x~t′,vϕ, 0]\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{\prime},\,v_{\phi},\,0\big] for the teacher’s and the auxiliary network’s predictions at that state, so that

vreal​(x~t′,t)−vϕ​(x~t′,t)=−1t​(x~real−x~aux).v_{\mathrm{real}}(\tilde{x}_{t}^{\prime},t)-v_{\phi}(\tilde{x}_{t}^{\prime},t)=-\frac{1}{t}\big(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real}}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}}\big). (44)

The noised prediction is affine in x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta}, so its Jacobian passes through to ∂x~θ/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta,

∇θℒDMD=−1−tt2​(∂x~θ∂θ)⊤​(x~real−x~aux).\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DMD}}=-\frac{1-t}{t^{2}}\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\!\top}\big(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real}}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}}\big). (45)

With this convention, Equation (45) is Equation (28) with

x~rwd=x~real,x~base=x~aux,Wreg=0,Wrwd=1−t2​t2,ω=1.\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real}},\quad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}},\quad W_{\mathrm{reg}}=0,\quad W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\frac{1-t}{2t^{2}},\quad\omega=1. (46)

The two distillation implementations therefore differ mainly in (i) how the instantaneous velocity of the current model distribution pθp_{\theta} is estimated and (ii) the state at which x~real\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{real}} and x~base\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}} are evaluated.

  • •

    DMD parameterises the instantaneous velocity with a second network vϕv_{\phi} with parameters ϕ\phi, fitted online to the student’s samples by Equation (9), and sets x~base=x~aux\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}} at x~t′\tilde{x}_{t}^{\prime}. It uses the clean-end prediction because Equation (45) uses ∂x~θ/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta; varying tt distributes the update over noise levels but always trains the same map uθ​(⋅,t,0)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,0) to the endpoint of the trajectory.

  • •

    MeanFlow induces the instantaneous velocity, computing vind=uold+J⁡[uold,t,r]v_{\mathrm{ind}}=u_{\mathrm{old}}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big] from the network itself, and sets x~base=x~ind,r\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind},r}, whose r=0r=0 case is the clean end Equation (38). Since vindv_{\mathrm{ind}} is defined at every queried (t,r)(t,r), this restriction disappears; Equation (42) uses ∂x~θ,r/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta,r}/\partial\theta, and resampling rr at every update trains uθ​(⋅,t,r)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,r) for all r∈[0,t]r\in[0,t].

4.3 Adaptation to Few-Step Models

The methods of §3.2 are built on an instantaneous velocity, where the clean predictions in §4 are x~θ(i)=X⁡[x~t(i),vθ, 0]\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},\,v_{\theta},\,0\big], Equation (30) uses ∂x~θ(i)/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}/\partial\theta, and the anchors apply the same map to voldv_{\mathrm{old}} or vrealv_{\mathrm{real}}. A few-step policy instead outputs an average velocity uθ​(x~t,t,r)u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r). To evaluate Equation (30), the velocity in Equation (21) can be replaced by a velocity recovered from uθu_{\theta}, and the anchors by the matching predictions of uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} or the teacher. Therefore, methods differ in which predictions and anchors they use. A rollout sample x^(i)\hat{x}^{(i)} is already a sample and needs no reconstruction, and the teacher prediction Equation (36) remains instantaneous, so only x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} and the old-policy anchors need to be rebuilt.

Building anchors with u-prediction.

The direct substitution queries only the r=0r=0 edge of the domain {0≤r≤t≤1}\{0\leq r\leq t\leq 1\} of the flow map,

x~θ,u=X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,0), 0]=x~t−t​uθ​(x~t,t,0).\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{u}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,0),\,0\big]=\tilde{x}_{t}-t\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,0). (47)

The policy velocity vθ​(x~t,t)v_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t) in §4 is replaced by uθ​(x~t,t,0)u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,0), and the old policy is treated in the same way,

x~old,u=X⁡[x~t,uold​(x~t,t,0), 0]=x~t−t​uold​(x~t,t,0).\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,0),\,0\big]=\tilde{x}_{t}-t\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,0). (48)

The current prediction of Equation (30) is then x~θ←x~θ,u\tilde{x}_{\theta}\leftarrow\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{u}}, and both the regression and the baseline anchor are x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}, or x~base=sg⁡(x~θ,u)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{u}}) in the AWM case where the baseline follows the policy.

The Jacobian in Equation (28) is then ∂x~θ,u/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{u}}/\partial\theta, so each update trains only uθ​(⋅,t,0)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,0). The sampler Equation (5) uses x^θ,r=x^θ,t−(t−r)​uθ​(⋅,t,r)\hat{x}_{\theta,r}=\hat{x}_{\theta,t}-(t-r)\,u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,r) with rr not necessarily zero. Therefore, in u-prediction, the flow map is trained only on its r=0r=0 edge and leaves the entries with r≠0r\neq 0, which the sampler uses, without a gradient.

Building anchors with v-prediction.

In u-prediction, the instantaneous velocity is not used. Alternatively, Equation (30) keeps x~θ=X⁡[x~t,v, 0]\tilde{x}_{\theta}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,v,\,0\big], and the remaining question is how to construct vv from a network that outputs an average velocity. Following Example 5, there are two constructions.

Self-induced velocity. Equation (37) recovers the instantaneous velocity from the average velocity itself, as in MeanFlowNFT, which applies DiffusionNFT, regressed on the forward (noising) process, to an average-velocity policy (Huang et al., 2026b). The current prediction adds the same detached JJ to uθu_{\theta}, which gives the v-prediction

x~θ,v=X⁡[x~t,uθ+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0]=x~t−t⁡(uθ+J⁡[uold,t,r]),\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big]=\tilde{x}_{t}-t\big(u_{\theta}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big]\big), (49)

and the old policy gives the self-induced anchor Equation (38),

x~ind=X⁡[x~t,vind, 0]=x~t−t⁡(uold+J⁡[uold,t,r]),\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,v_{\mathrm{ind}},\,0\big]=\tilde{x}_{t}-t\big(u_{\mathrm{old}}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big]\big), (50)

so that x~θ,v−x~ind=−t⁡(uθ−uold)\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}=-t(u_{\theta}-u_{\mathrm{old}}). Since JJ is detached, Equation (41) still holds; JJ shifts the prediction but does not change its Jacobian. The pair (t,r)(t,r) is the input of the network and rr is resampled at every update, so every uθ​(⋅,t,r)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,r) on the trajectory enters ∂x~θ/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta. The loss itself is still evaluated at r=0r=0; rr enters only as a network input and through JJ, and does not change the level at which Equation (30) is evaluated.

Auxiliary velocity. The instantaneous velocity can instead be parameterised by a second network vϕv_{\phi}, fitted by Equation (9) to the samples of the model, so that its population target is the marginal velocity of pθp_{\theta},

vϕ​(x~t,t)≈𝔼x^∼pθ,ϵ​[ϵ−x^∣x~t],x~t=(1−t)​x^+t​ϵ.v_{\phi}(\tilde{x}_{t},t)\;\approx\;\mathbb{E}_{\,\hat{x}\sim p_{\theta},\,\epsilon}\big[\epsilon-\hat{x}\mid\tilde{x}_{t}\big],\qquad\tilde{x}_{t}=(1-t)\,\hat{x}+t\,\epsilon. (51)

In the RL setting of §3.2, however, the rollouts are samples from poldp_{\mathrm{old}} and not from pθp_{\theta}, so the target is the marginal velocity of poldp_{\mathrm{old}},

vϕ​(x~t,t)≈𝔼x^∼pold,ϵ​[ϵ−x^∣x~t],x~t=(1−t)​x^+t​ϵ.v_{\phi}(\tilde{x}_{t},t)\;\approx\;\mathbb{E}_{\,\hat{x}\sim p_{\mathrm{old}},\,\epsilon}\big[\epsilon-\hat{x}\mid\tilde{x}_{t}\big],\qquad\tilde{x}_{t}=(1-t)\,\hat{x}+t\,\epsilon. (52)

Its clean prediction x~aux=X⁡[x~t,vϕ, 0]\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,v_{\phi},\,0\big] is detached, like x~ind\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}, and serves only as an anchor. The current prediction cannot be computed from vϕv_{\phi}, since ∂x~θ/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta would then vanish and the reward would not affect the policy. It is therefore computed from uθu_{\theta}, e.g., as x~θ,u\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{u}}, x~θ,v\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}, or the JJ-free (t,r)(t,r) query X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big], i.e., the transport of x~t\tilde{x}_{t} to the clean end with the average velocity queried at (t,r)(t,r), which has the same Jacobian as x~θ,v\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}. Its old-policy counterpart is x~ind\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}} with JJ dropped, x~ind|J=0=X⁡[x~t,uold​(x~t,t,r), 0]{\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}|_{J=0}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]. The self-induced construction requires a Jacobian-vector product with a stop-gradient; the auxiliary construction requires a second network and optimiser that must follow a moving target.

Within the framework, a few-step method therefore does not introduce a new loss; it specifies how the four points of Equation (30) are computed and which entries uθ​(⋅,t,r)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,r) of the flow map receive a gradient through ∂x~θ/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta. Table 1 summarises the three forms.

The first column trains only the r=0r=0 edge of the map; the second and the third train all of it. The third column uses the auxiliary velocity only for the baseline and computes x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} and x~reg\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}} at the same (t,r)(t,r) without JJ; x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} has the same Jacobian as x~θ,v\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}.

Example 6 (DiffusionNFT with u-prediction).

With u-prediction, the weights and the rewarded sample of Equation (35) are unchanged, Wreg=Wrwd=β2/t2W_{\mathrm{reg}}=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\beta^{2}/t^{2} and x~rwd=x^\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\hat{x}, and both anchors become the r=0r=0 prediction of the old policy,

x~θ=x~θ,u=X⁡[x~t,uθ, 0],x~reg=x~base=x~old,u=X⁡[x~t,uold, 0].\tilde{x}_{\theta}=\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{u}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta},\,0\big],\qquad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}},\,0\big]. (53)

Starting from the two squares of Equation (30),

ℒreg=Wreg​‖X⁡[x~t,uθ, 0]−X⁡[x~t,uold, 0]‖2,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}=W_{\mathrm{reg}}\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta},\,0\big]-X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}},\,0\big]\right\rVert^{2}, (54)
ℒrwd=Wrwd​‖X⁡[x~t,uθ, 0]−sg⁡(X⁡[x~t,uθ, 0]+gu)‖2,\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}}=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta},\,0\big]-\operatorname{sg}\big(X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta},\,0\big]+g_{\mathrm{u}}\big)\right\rVert^{2}, (55)

where x~θ=X⁡[x~t,uθ, 0]\tilde{x}_{\theta}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta},\,0\big] and gu=ω⁡(x^−X⁡[x~t,uold, 0])g_{\mathrm{u}}=\omega\big(\hat{x}-X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}},\,0\big]\big). The copy of x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} inside sg\operatorname{sg} does not cancel with the copy outside. No JJ appears, the two anchors coincide, and ∂x~θ/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta involves only r=0r=0. This is DiffusionNFT evaluated on the r=0r=0 edge (t,0)(t,0).

Example 7 (DiffusionNFT with v-prediction).

The decomposition Equation (35) carries over, and the self-induced construction below keeps x~reg=x~base\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}. The remaining choice is how to recover the instantaneous velocity used in Equation (21) from an average-velocity network, and Equation (49)–(52) give two ways to do so. The first is to use the self-induced velocity vind=uold+J⁡[uold,t,r]v_{\mathrm{ind}}=u_{\mathrm{old}}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big], which adds the Jacobian-vector term J⁡[uold,t,r]J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big] to every prediction of the policy and of the old-policy anchor, as in Equation (49)–(50); this construction gives the MeanFlowNFT-style variant (Huang et al., 2026b). The second is to fit an auxiliary network vϕv_{\phi} to the marginal velocity of the rollouts, Equation (51)–(52), and compute the baseline as x~aux\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}}, which leads to DMDNFT. In both cases the current prediction x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} is computed from uθu_{\theta}, since otherwise ∂x~θ/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta would vanish.

MeanFlowNFT queries the network at (t,r)(t,r) with 0≤r≤t0\leq r\leq t, so every prediction of the policy is a v-prediction. Following prior directional-difference flow-map work (Nie et al., 2026; Gu et al., 2026), the MeanFlowNFT construction evaluates one derivative on the frozen old policy and shares it between the current and the old policy (Huang et al., 2026b), which gives the four points

x~θ\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\theta} =x~θ,v=X⁡[x~t,uθ+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0],\displaystyle=\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big], (56)
x~reg=x~base\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}} =x~ind=X⁡[x~t,uold+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0]\displaystyle=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big]
x~rwd\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}} =x^.\displaystyle=\hat{x}.

Starting from the two squares of Equation (30),

ℒreg\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}} =Wreg​‖X⁡[x~t,uθ+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0]−X⁡[x~t,uold+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0]‖2\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{reg}}\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big]-X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big]\right\rVert^{2} (57)
=Wreg​‖X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]−X⁡[x~t,uold​(x~t,t,r), 0]‖2,\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{reg}}\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]-X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]\right\rVert^{2},
ℒrwd\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}} =Wrwd​‖X⁡[x~t,uθ+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0]−sg⁡(X⁡[x~t,uθ+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0]+gv)‖2\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big]-\operatorname{sg}\big(X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big]+g_{\mathrm{v}}\big)\right\rVert^{2} (58)
=Wrwd​‖X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]−sg⁡(X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]+gv)‖2.\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]-\operatorname{sg}\big(X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]+g_{\mathrm{v}}\big)\right\rVert^{2}.

The prediction x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} is still the v-prediction of Equation (56). In ℒreg\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}, the shared detached JJ cancels between the current and old-policy predictions; in ℒrwd\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}}, it cancels between the two copies of the current prediction. The reward displacement still contains the old-policy prediction,

gv=ω⁡(x^−X⁡[x~t,uold+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0]),g_{\mathrm{v}}=\omega\big(\hat{x}-X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big]\big),

and therefore retains JJ. Since JJ is detached, the Jacobian is that of X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]. Resampling rr then updates the family uθ​(⋅,t,r)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,r) instead of only its r=0r=0 edge.

DMDNFT is the alternative construction. In the losses, only the baseline changes, with vϕv_{\phi} fitted online to the old-policy rollouts by Equation (52). The current prediction is still computed from uθu_{\theta}, since substituting vϕv_{\phi} would give ∂x~θ,v/∂θ=0\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}/\partial\theta=0. As in Equation (41), JJ is detached, so

∂x~θ,v∂θ=∂∂θ​X​[x~t,uθ+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0]=∂∂θ​X​[x~t,uθ, 0].\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}}{\partial\theta}=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big]=\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta},\,0\big]. (59)

Therefore, the four points are

x~θ\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\theta} =X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0],\displaystyle=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big], (60)
x~reg\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}} =x~ind|J=0=X⁡[x~t,uold​(x~t,t,r), 0],\displaystyle={\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}|_{J=0}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big],
x~base\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}} =x~aux,\displaystyle=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}},
x~rwd\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}} =x^.\displaystyle=\hat{x}.
Example 8 (Few-step DiffusionOPSD).

DiffusionOPSD keeps the training scheme of DiffusionNFT but constructs the point toward which the policy should move, which requires a reward R⁡(𝒟⁡(⋅),c)R(\mathcal{D}(\cdot),c) that is differentiable with respect to the clean sample. Three clean points are constructed at one query state x~t(i)=AddNoise​(x^(i),t)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)}=\textsc{AddNoise}(\hat{x}^{(i)},t) at a small noise level tt (drawn from a law concentrated below 0.50.5, §6.1). The first is the old policy’s prediction at this state, given by Equation (24),

x~old(i)=X⁡[x~t(i),vold, 0].\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},\,v_{\mathrm{old}},\,0\big]. (61)

The other two points are obtained by MtgtM_{\mathrm{tgt}} normalised reward-gradient steps in xx-space, in the ascent and in the descent direction. Suppressing (i)(i) on the iterates and indexing them by [m][m], x~±[0]=x~old(i)\tilde{x}^{[0]}_{\pm}=\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}} and

x~±[m+1]=x~±[m]±h​∇R​(𝒟⁡(x~±[m]),c)‖∇R​(𝒟⁡(x~±[m]),c)‖+εg,h=η​κ​‖x~old(i)‖Mtgt,\tilde{x}^{[m+1]}_{\pm}=\tilde{x}^{[m]}_{\pm}\pm h\,\frac{\nabla R\big(\mathcal{D}(\tilde{x}^{[m]}_{\pm}),c\big)}{\left\lVert\nabla R\big(\mathcal{D}(\tilde{x}^{[m]}_{\pm}),c\big)\right\rVert+\varepsilon_{g}},\qquad h=\frac{\eta\,\kappa\,\left\lVert\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}\right\rVert}{M_{\mathrm{tgt}}}, (62)

for m=0,…,Mtgt−1m=0,\dots,M_{\mathrm{tgt}}-1, with a small floor εg>0\varepsilon_{g}>0, the relative trust radius κ>0\kappa>0 and the total step length η>0\eta>0 in units of that radius. Each iterate is projected onto the ball of radius κ​‖x~old(i)‖\kappa\left\lVert\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}\right\rVert around the anchor; before projection, Mtgt​hM_{\mathrm{tgt}}h is η\eta times that radius. The final points x~±(i)=sg⁡(x~±[Mtgt])\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\pm}=\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}^{[M_{\mathrm{tgt}}]}_{\pm}) are detached. For η≤1\eta\leq 1 the projection is inactive, and their displacements are

Δrwdx~(i)±:=x~(i)±−x~(i)old=±h∑m=0Mtgt−1∇R​(𝒟⁡(x~±[m]),c)‖∇R​(𝒟⁡(x~±[m]),c)‖+εg.\Delta_{\mathrm{rwd}}\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\pm}:=\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\pm}-\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}=\pm h\sum_{m=0}^{M_{\mathrm{tgt}}-1}\frac{\nabla R\big(\mathcal{D}(\tilde{x}^{[m]}_{\pm}),c\big)}{\left\lVert\nabla R\big(\mathcal{D}(\tilde{x}^{[m]}_{\pm}),c\big)\right\rVert+\varepsilon_{g}}. (63)

The labels ±\pm indicate the directions of construction. We construct the loss function in three steps:

(i) Fitting reuses the two xx-space branches of Equation (26), now regressed onto the constructed points instead of the rollout sample:

x~θ±\displaystyle\tilde{x}^{\pm}_{\theta} =x~old(i)±β⁡(x~θ(i)−x~old(i)),\displaystyle=\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}\pm\beta\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}\big), (64)
ℒOPSD=𝔼i​[ℒOPSD(i)],ℒOPSD(i)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}=\mathbb{E}_{\,i}\big[\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}\big],\qquad\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{OPSD}} =a+​‖x~θ+−x~+(i)‖2+a−​‖x~θ−−x~−(i)‖2,\displaystyle=a_{+}\left\lVert\tilde{x}^{+}_{\theta}-\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{+}\right\rVert^{2}+a_{-}\left\lVert\tilde{x}^{-}_{\theta}-\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{-}\right\rVert^{2},

with a+=r^(i)/γ+a_{+}=\hat{r}^{(i)}/\gamma_{+} and a−=(1−r^(i))/γ−a_{-}=(1-\hat{r}^{(i)})/\gamma_{-} non-negative and detached, r^(i)\hat{r}^{(i)} the weight of Equation (18) and γ±=max⁡{sg⁡meansp⁡[|x~θ±−x~±(i)|],εγ}\gamma_{\pm}=\max\{\operatorname{sg}\,\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[|\tilde{x}^{\pm}_{\theta}-\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\pm}|\right],\varepsilon_{\gamma}\} the adaptive normalisers with floor εγ>0\varepsilon_{\gamma}>0, and where meansp⁡[⋅]\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\cdot\right] denotes the per-sample mean, i.e., the average over the NN elements of one sample.

(ii) To decouple the loss into Equation (30) with gradient form Equation (28), note that the two branches are reflections of each other about the anchor, so both residuals are affine in the same displacement x~θ(i)−x~old(i)\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}. Expanding the squares of ℒOPSD(i)\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{OPSD}} and discarding the θ\theta-free remainder therefore splits it into one square and two inner products, each written directly on the three constructed points:

ℒOPSD(i)=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}= β2​(a++a−)​‖x~θ(i)−x~old(i)‖2⏟self-regression\displaystyle\underbrace{\beta^{2}(a_{+}+a_{-})\,\left\lVert\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}\right\rVert^{2}}_{\text{self-regression}} (65)
−2​β​a+​(x~θ(i)−x~old(i))⊤​Δrwd​x~+(i)⏟reward augmentation, positive+2​β​a−​(x~θ(i)−x~old(i))⊤​Δrwd​x~−(i)⏟reward augmentation, negative+const,\displaystyle-\underbrace{2\beta a_{+}\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}\big)^{\!\top}\Delta_{\mathrm{rwd}}\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{+}}_{\text{reward augmentation, positive}}+\underbrace{2\beta a_{-}\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}}\big)^{\!\top}\Delta_{\mathrm{rwd}}\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{-}}_{\text{reward augmentation, negative}}\;+\;\mathrm{const},

the constant being a+​‖Δrwd​x~+(i)‖2+a−​‖Δrwd​x~−(i)‖2a_{+}\left\lVert\Delta_{\mathrm{rwd}}\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{+}\right\rVert^{2}+a_{-}\left\lVert\Delta_{\mathrm{rwd}}\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{-}\right\rVert^{2}, which has no gradient. Differentiating gives three terms with the same Jacobian,

(66)

Equations (65) and (66) contain one self-regression term and two reward-augmentation terms, indexed by k=1,2k=1,2:

x~reg(i)=x~(i)old,Wreg=Wrwd=β2(a++a−),\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}=\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}},\qquad W_{\mathrm{reg}}=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\beta^{2}(a_{+}+a_{-}), (67)
x~(i)rwd,1=x~(i)+,x~(i)base,1=x~(i)old,ω1=a+β⁡(a++a−),\displaystyle\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{rwd},1}=\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{+},\quad\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{base},1}=\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{old}},\quad\omega_{1}=\frac{a_{+}}{\beta(a_{+}+a_{-})},
