The self-regression is toward the old policy’s prediction, as in Equation (35). The two reward terms share this baseline, x~base,1(i)=x~base,2(i)=x~reg(i)\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{base},1}=\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{base},2}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}, and differ only in the constructed rewarded point x~rwd,k(i)\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{rwd},k} and its signed reward coefficient. The signs of ω1\omega_{1} and ω2\omega_{2} are not determined by the endpoint advantage A(i)A^{(i)}; no advantage is defined for the constructed points. They are fixed to be non-negative for the ascent branch and non-positive for the descent branch.

Applying Equation (29) to each reward term separately gives a loss with gradient Equation (66), in the form Equation (30) with two reward squares,

ℒOPSD(i)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{OPSD}} =ℒreg(i)+ℒrwd,1(i)+ℒrwd,2(i),\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{reg}}+\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{rwd},1}+\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{rwd},2}, (68)
ℒreg(i)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{reg}} =Wreg​‖x~θ(i)−x~reg(i)‖2,\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{reg}}\left\lVert\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}\right\rVert^{2},
ℒrwd,k(i)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{rwd},k} =Wrwd‖x~θ(i)−sg(x~θ(i)+g(i)k)‖2,k=1,2,\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}\left\lVert\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}-\operatorname{sg}\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}+g^{(i)}_{k}\big)\right\rVert^{2},\qquad k=1,2,

The branch magnitudes satisfy |ω1|+|ω2|=1/β|\omega_{1}|+|\omega_{2}|=1/\beta, so r^(i)\hat{r}^{(i)} redistributes that total between the two branches. It can also change the common weight W=β2​(a++a−)W=\beta^{2}(a_{+}+a_{-}) whenever γ+≠γ−\gamma_{+}\neq\gamma_{-}. At r^(i)→1\hat{r}^{(i)}\to 1 only the ascent displacement remains, at r^(i)→0\hat{r}^{(i)}\to 0 only the descent displacement remains, and the self-regression and two reward-augmentation contributions sum to zero at x~θ(i)=x~reg(i)+g1(i)+g2(i)\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)}+g^{(i)}_{1}+g^{(i)}_{2}.

(iii) For an average-velocity policy we take the v-prediction form of Equations (49)–(50), as in Example 7. Suppressing (i)(i) and writing J=J⁡[uold,t,r]J=J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big], the corresponding quantities are

x~θ\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\theta} =X⁡[x~t,uθ+J, 0],\displaystyle=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J,\,0\big], (69)
x~reg=x~base,1=x~base,2\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base},1}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base},2} =x~ind=X⁡[x~t,uold+J, 0],\displaystyle=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}+J,\,0\big],
x~rwd,1\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd},1} =x~+,x~rwd,2=x~−,\displaystyle=\tilde{x}_{+},\qquad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd},2}=\tilde{x}_{-},

where the gradient steps Equation (62) are not started at x~ind\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}, which contains JJ, but at the r=0r=0 prediction x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}} of Equation (48), and only the resulting displacement is transferred to the anchor:

Δ=x~old,u−x~ind,x~±=[apply Equation (62) from x~±[0]=x~old,u]−Δ.\Delta=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}},\qquad\tilde{x}_{\pm}=\big[\text{apply \text{Equation}~(\ref{eq:opsd-target}) from }\tilde{x}^{[0]}_{\pm}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}\big]-\Delta. (70)

The weights are unchanged. We expand the three squares of Equation (68) in turn.

The self-regression is the self-regression square of Equation (57):

ℒreg=Wreg​‖X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]−X⁡[x~t,uold​(x~t,t,r), 0]‖2.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}=W_{\mathrm{reg}}\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]-X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]\right\rVert^{2}. (71)

Both copies of JJ are the same detached estimate computed from uoldu_{\mathrm{old}}, so they cancel.

The two reward squares are

ℒrwd,k\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd},k} =Wrwd​‖X⁡[x~t,uθ+J, 0]−sg⁡(X⁡[x~t,uθ+J, 0]+gk)‖2\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J,\,0\big]-\operatorname{sg}\big(X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}+J,\,0\big]+g_{k}\big)\right\rVert^{2} (72)
=Wrwd‖X[x~t,uθ(x~t,t,r), 0]−sg(X[x~t,uθ(x~t,t,r), 0]+gk)‖2,k=1,2,\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]-\operatorname{sg}\big(X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]+g_{k}\big)\right\rVert^{2},\qquad k=1,2,

where, by Equation (69),

gk=ωk​(x~rwd,k−x~base,k),i.e.g1=ω1​(x~+−x~ind),g2=ω2​(x~−−x~ind).g_{k}=\omega_{k}\big(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd},k}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base},k}\big),\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad g_{1}=\omega_{1}\big(\tilde{x}_{+}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}\big),\quad g_{2}=\omega_{2}\big(\tilde{x}_{-}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}\big). (73)

Because x~±−x~ind\tilde{x}_{\pm}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}} is constructed from x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}} by Equation (70), JJ also cancels from both reward squares (Appendix C). Hence no square of the loss contains JJ, Equation (68) depends only on x~θ=X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]\tilde{x}_{\theta}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big], x~reg=x~ind|J=0\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}={\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}|_{J=0}} and the JJ-free gkg_{k}, and by Equation (41) the Jacobian is that of X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]. FewStepOPSD in v-prediction form thus reduces to the JJ-free (t,r)(t,r) query of §4.3 for every (t,r)(t,r), not only at r=0r=0.

Example 9 (ReFL as Few-step DiffusionOPSD).

Reward feedback learning (ReFL) backpropagates the gradient of a differentiable reward through a single late denoising step. Classic ReFL stops a rollout of the old-policy sampler at a small noise level tt without gradient and lets the policy predict the clean sample from that state with one network evaluation; as in Example 8, we instead evaluate the network at the re-noised state x~t(i)=AddNoise​(x^(i),t)\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)}=\textsc{AddNoise}(\hat{x}^{(i)},t) and maximise the reward of the resulting prediction,

ℒReFL=−λ​𝔼i,t​[R⁡(𝒟⁡(x~θ(i)),c)],x~θ(i)=X⁡[x~t(i),vθ, 0],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ReFL}}=-\lambda\,\mathbb{E}_{\,i,\,t}\Big[R\big(\mathcal{D}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}),c\big)\Big],\qquad\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t}^{(i)},\,v_{\theta},\,0\big], (74)

with a loss weight λ>0\lambda>0. Only this final evaluation is differentiated,

∇θℒReFL(i)=−λ(∂x~θ(i)∂θ)⊤∇R(𝒟(x~θ(i)),c),\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}^{(i)}_{\mathrm{ReFL}}=-\lambda\left(\frac{\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\!\top}\nabla R\big(\mathcal{D}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)}),c\big), (75)

where ∇R​(𝒟​(⋅),c)\nabla R(\mathcal{D}(\cdot),c) is the gradient with respect to the clean sample, as in Equation (62). The backward pass therefore propagates through the decoder and the reward model.

Consider Equation (68) with a single reward-gradient step, Mtgt=1M_{\mathrm{tgt}}=1, no self-regression, Wreg=0W_{\mathrm{reg}}=0, and only the ascent term ℒrwd,1\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd},1}, with any detached Wrwd,ω1>0W_{\mathrm{rwd}},\omega_{1}>0. x~base,1\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base},1} =x~ind=X⁡[x~t,uold+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0],\displaystyle=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big], (78)

The reward augmentation loss is Equation (72) with this g1g_{1},

ℒrwd,1=Wrwd​‖X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]−sg⁡(X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]+g1)‖2,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd},1}=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}\left\lVert X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]-\operatorname{sg}\big(X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big]+g_{1}\big)\right\rVert^{2}, (79)

whose reward augmentation moves the prediction X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big] at each sampled (t,r)(t,r) along ∇R​(𝒟​(x~old,u),c)\nabla R(\mathcal{D}(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}),c). Apart from WrwdW_{\mathrm{rwd}} and the velocity penalty, a step requires one detached rollout, two forward passes of uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} (at rr and at r=0r=0), one reward gradient, and one forward and backward pass of uθu_{\theta}; JJ cancels, because it shifts both ends of the displacement equally, and is therefore dropped. With JJ dropped and r=0r=0 we have x~ind=x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}, which is the u-form. At a generic rr, only the current prediction and its anchor use (t,r)(t,r); the decoder and the reward are still evaluated at the clean prediction x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}, while the resulting displacement trains uθ​(⋅,t,r)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,r).

5 Implementation

The framework of §4 is implemented as one base trainer whose method step runs one outer iteration. Each trainer of §§5.3–5.6 is a subclass that overrides a few stage methods, and the instantaneous-velocity estimator of §4.3, v-ind or v-aux, is a separate object passed to the trainer. Here v-ind uses the MeanFlow identity with the shared old-policy correction JJ to construct an instantaneous velocity from an average velocity, whereas v-aux uses an auxiliary velocity to approximate the instantaneous velocity of the old-policy rollout distribution poldp_{\mathrm{old}} (which DMD takes to be pθp_{\theta}), as in Equation (52). Stages 1 and 2 below operate on groups, since they produce and score the KK members of a prompt, and keep the index (i)(i) as in §§3–4.3. From Stage 3 onward the framework acts on one member at a time. The prediction, the three anchors and the three weights are per-sample quantities; the index (i)(i) is omitted in the equations and in the loss terms ℒreg\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}, ℒrwd\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}}, and becomes the leading batch axis in code.

5.1 A General Training Step

One outer iteration fixes an old policy uoldu_{\mathrm{old}}, rolls it out, scores the rollouts, and then takes one gradient step on the mean over nitn_{\mathrm{it}} queries of

ℒ⁡(θ)=𝔼⁡[Wreg​meansp​[(x~θ−x~reg)2]+Wrwd​meansp​[(x~θ−sg⁡(x~θ+g))2]+λKL​ℒKL],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\Big[W_{\mathrm{reg}}\,\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}\big)^{2}\right]+W_{\mathrm{rwd}}\,\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}+g)\big)^{2}\right]+\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}\Big], (80)

where x^(i)=Rollout​(ϵ(i),uold,c)\hat{x}^{(i)}=\textsc{Rollout}(\epsilon^{(i)},u_{\mathrm{old}},c) is a detached rollout of prompt cc. The per-sample mean meansp⁡[⋅]\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\cdot\right] rescales every weight WW by 1/N1/N relative to the squared norms of §4.2; this constant is absorbed into the learning rate. ℒKL\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}} is the velocity penalty of Stage 4 with weight λKL\lambda_{\mathrm{KL}}, evaluated on the same method-specific query.

The training workflow.

One outer iteration consists of five operations, executed in order; the four method-specific stages of §1 are operations 1, 2, 4 and the loss inside 4, while operations 3 and 5 are shared bookkeeping.

  1. (i)

    Rollout: the old policy uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} samples KK members per prompt with the sampler of Stage 1, and the endpoints x^(i)\hat{x}^{(i)} are detached.

  2. (ii)

    Reward and advantage: each endpoint is decoded and scored, R(i)=R⁡(𝒟⁡(x^(i)),c)R^{(i)}=R\big(\mathcal{D}(\hat{x}^{(i)}),c\big), and Stage 2 turns the rewards into the advantage A(i)A^{(i)} and the mixing weight r^(i)\hat{r}^{(i)} (Equation (83), Equation (84)).

  3. (iii)

    Auxiliary fit: a trainer that uses the auxiliary velocity vϕv_{\phi} first fits it to these rollouts with the flow-matching loss Equation (88) for nfmn_{\mathrm{fm}} steps, before the policy is updated; the other trainers skip this step.

  4. (iv)

    Training loss: nitn_{\mathrm{it}} inner iterations each draw a query (Stage 3 (i)), compute the prediction, anchors and coefficients (Stage 3 (ii)–(iv)), and accumulate the gradient of Equation (80) (Stage 4); one optimiser step is taken on their mean.

  5. (v)

    Refresh: uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} becomes the EMA of uθu_{\theta}, and the next iteration rolls out with it.

In code, this is the method step of the base trainer in Section 5.1, one block per operation: rollout, advantage, estimator.fit, the loop over queries with anchors, weights and loss, and refresh_old. Each Query object is a view of the batch for one method-specific training query; fields it does not set, such as the advantage, are read from the batch.

A trainer of §§5.3–5.6 is a subclass that implements anchors and weights, and overrides another hook only where it changes that stage (Table 2). anchors returns the prediction and three anchors of Equation (90), with a tuple of rewarded anchors for FewStepOPSD; weights returns the detached coefficients, with ω\omega signed and a tuple for FewStepOPSD, and loss is shared by every trainer except FewStepOPSD and ReFL, which override it. The named methods of §6 other than ReFL differ from their family only in the estimator they use.

5.2 Introduction to the Key Stages

This subsection describes, for each stage of Section 5.1, the default computation, its cost, and the choices that the framework determines.

Stage 1: the rollout operator

Let Rollout denote the sampler. We distinguish two cases.

(a) Sample-independent rollout. For every trainer except the FewStepOPSD family, the group members of a prompt are i.i.d. draws:

x^(i)=Rollout(ϵ(i),uold,c),ϵ(i)∼iid𝒩(0,I),i=1,…,K,\hat{x}^{(i)}\;=\;\textsc{Rollout}\big(\epsilon^{(i)},\,u_{\mathrm{old}},\,c\big),\qquad\epsilon^{(i)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{iid}}}{{\sim}}\mathcal{N}(0,I),\quad i=1,\dots,K, (81)

i.e. the only stochasticity is the initial noise (and, for the stochastic sampler below, the per-step renoise). Members do not interact.

The sampler uses the old policy uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} and not uθu_{\theta}, as indicated by the argument of Equation (81). One old policy is fixed per outer iteration, so that the rewarded endpoint x^(i)\hat{x}^{(i)}, the regression anchor and the baseline anchor all refer to the same distribution, as required in §4.2, where x~reg(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}^{(i)} and x~base(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}^{(i)} must be evaluated at the state from which x~θ(i)\tilde{x}_{\theta}^{(i)} is computed. If the samples were drawn from uθu_{\theta}, the reward would be evaluated on a distribution different from the one described by the anchors, and A(i)A^{(i)} would not be the advantage of the policy that defines the anchors.

(b) Reward-coupled rollout. For reward-coupled rollout, FewStepOPSD extends the rollout with the reward,

{x^(i),x~oldu,(i),x~±(i)}i=1K=Rollout​(ϵ(i),uold,R,c).\big\{\hat{x}^{(i)},\,\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old}}^{\mathrm{u},(i)},\,\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\pm}\big\}_{i=1}^{K}\;=\;\textsc{Rollout}\big(\epsilon^{(i)},\,u_{\mathrm{old}},\,R,\,c\big). (82)

The members remain i.i.d.; the reward does not couple different members. For each member, the sampler of Equation (81) runs unchanged. The reward-coupled construction then applies Equation (62) from the r=0r=0 prediction x~oldu,(i)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old}}^{\mathrm{u},(i)} and transfers the resulting displacements to the anchor by Equation (70), giving x~±(i)\tilde{x}^{(i)}_{\pm} together with the endpoint.

In code, rollout defaults to (a) with the deterministic sampler; FewStepGRPO overrides it with the stochastic sampler of §5.3, keeping the transitions, and FewStepOPSD appends the reward-coupled construction of (b).

Stage 2: reward and group advantage

The generic advantage Equation (12) takes both the mean and the standard deviation over the group; the implementation changes the population of the standard deviation. With R(i)=R⁡(𝒟⁡(x^(i)),c)R^{(i)}=R\big(\mathcal{D}(\hat{x}^{(i)}),c\big) the endpoint reward (𝒟\mathcal{D} the VAE decoder), the advantage is

A(i)=R(i)−R¯cstd⁡({R}ℬ)+10−4,R¯c=1|Hc|​∑R∈HcR,{\;A^{(i)}=\frac{R^{(i)}-\bar{R}_{c}}{\operatorname{std}\big(\{R\}_{\mathcal{B}}\big)+10^{-4}},\qquad\bar{R}_{c}=\frac{1}{|H_{c}|}\sum_{R\in H_{c}}R,\;} (83)

where HcH_{c} is the set of rewards of prompt cc in the current outer iteration and {R}ℬ\{R\}_{\mathcal{B}} is the current global batch gathered across all ranks. The numerator and denominator use different populations. The per-prompt mean reduces the effect of prompt difficulty, and the global standard deviation avoids division by a near-zero value when all rewards in a group are equal.

The advantage is then compressed into a bounded mixing weight, generalising Equation (18) by replacing the unit clip range with a tunable cadvc_{\mathrm{adv}}:

r^(i)=clip⁡(A(i),−cadv,cadv)2​cadv+12∈[0,1].{\;\hat{r}^{(i)}\;=\;\frac{\operatorname{clip}\big(A^{(i)},\,-c_{\mathrm{adv}},\,c_{\mathrm{adv}}\big)}{2\,c_{\mathrm{adv}}}+\frac{1}{2}\;\in[0,1].\;} (84)

Here r^→1\hat{r}\to 1 means “far above the prompt’s mean”, r^→0\hat{r}\to 0 “far below”, r^=12\hat{r}=\tfrac{1}{2} “average”. This [0,1][0,1] form distinguishes the NFT/OPSD families from FewStepGRPO and FewStepAWM, which use clip⁡(A,−cadv,cadv)\operatorname{clip}(A,-c_{\mathrm{adv}},c_{\mathrm{adv}}) as a signed multiplier (§3.2); AA in Equation (97) and Equation (103) denotes this clipped value.

In code, advantage returns (A,r^)(A,\hat{r}); ReFL overrides it with r^≡1\hat{r}\equiv 1.

Stage 3: anchors and weights

The trainers differ mainly in this stage. It receives the detached rollout and returns the current prediction, the anchors and the detached coefficients; FewStepOPSD returns branch-indexed tuples for its rewarded anchors and ω\omega. We describe it in four parts, namely (i) the query levels, (ii) the two ways to compute the clean prediction, (iii) the two estimators of the instantaneous velocity that these predictions require, and (iv) the weights.

(i) The training query (t,r)(t,r). By default, a fresh pair (t,r)(t,r) is drawn at every inner iteration; “rr is resampled at every update” in §4.3 refers to this draw: tt is drawn from a selectable law (the maximum of two uniforms or a logit-normal), r|t∼U⁡(0,t)r\mid t\sim U(0,t), and a fixed fraction of the batch is set to r=tr=t and to r=0r=0. The three cases play different roles. For r=tr=t the interval has zero length and J≡0J\equiv 0, so the network query is instantaneous and the loss reduces to its instantaneous-velocity form; r=0r=0 trains the one-step generator and gives JJ its largest prefactor t−rt-r; the generic case lets ∂x~θ/∂θ\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta reach uθ​(⋅,t,r)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,r) for every rr in between, as required by the second column of Table 1.

(ii) The u- and v-predictions. Except for the replayed transition score of FewStepGRPO, the implemented reward losses evaluate Equation (21) at the clean level r=0r=0, but the network outputs the average velocity uθ​(x~t,t,r)u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r) instead of the instantaneous velocity required by the map. Using uθu_{\theta} directly gives the u-form:

x~θ=x~θ,u=X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,0), 0](u-form).{\;\tilde{x}_{\theta}=\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{u}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,0),\,0\big]\;}\qquad\text{(u-form)}. (85)

Adding the detached correction of Equation (37) gives the v-form; since the prediction carries the gradient, v-ind builds it with the self-induced velocity, i.e.,

x~θ=x~θ,v=X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r)+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0](v-form, v-ind).{\;\tilde{x}_{\theta}=\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big]\;}\qquad\text{(v-form, {v-ind})}. (86)

As in Equation (37), JJ is computed from uoldu_{\mathrm{old}}, so that a single estimate can be shared by all predictions, as required in (iii). Since JJ is detached, by Equation (41) the Jacobian of the v-form x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} is that of X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r), 0]X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big].

For the anchors x~base\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}, x~reg\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}} and x~rwd\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}, there are two alternatives in v-form, namely v-aux and v-ind.

(iii) Estimating the instantaneous velocity. There are two estimators of the instantaneous velocity, following MeanFlow (a.k.a. v-ind) and DMD (a.k.a. v-aux), respectively.

Self-induced vindv_{\mathrm{ind}}, with shared JJ (v-ind). The v-form needs JJ only as a detached vector. The directional-difference estimate, for a step size εcd>0\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}}>0, is

J⁡[uold,t,r]=(t−r)​uold​(x~t+εcd​vcond,t+εcd,r)−uold​(x~t−εcd​vcond,t−εcd,r)2​εcd.J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big]=(t-r)\,\frac{u_{\mathrm{old}}\!\big(\tilde{x}_{t}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}}v_{\mathrm{cond}},t+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}},r\big)-u_{\mathrm{old}}\!\big(\tilde{x}_{t}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}}v_{\mathrm{cond}},t-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}},r\big)}{2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}}}. (87)

For r=tr=t the prefactor t−rt-r makes it zero. It requires two additional forward passes of uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} per query, and one estimate is shared by the current prediction and the anchors, so the correction cancels in the self-regression difference x~θ−x~reg\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}} and across sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot), as discussed in Example 7.

Auxiliary vϕv_{\phi}, trained online (v-aux). vϕv_{\phi} is instead trained at every update by plain flow matching on the current rollout pool,

ℒaux=meansp⁡[(vϕ​(x~t,t)−vcond)2],x~t=AddNoise​(x^,t),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{aux}}=\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\big(v_{\phi}(\tilde{x}_{t},t)-v_{\mathrm{cond}}\big)^{2}\right],\qquad\tilde{x}_{t}=\textsc{AddNoise}(\hat{x},t), (88)

running nfmn_{\mathrm{fm}} steps of Equation (88) per outer iteration, before the policy update. The auxiliary-to-policy optimiser-step ratio is nfm:1n_{\mathrm{fm}}:1 (nfm=5n_{\mathrm{fm}}=5 in §6). This requires no extra rollout and no JJ, but it requires a second network and optimiser that must follow a target that changes with the policy, as stated in Example 7.

Section 5.2 implements the two instantaneous-velocity estimators as estimator objects. Their method fields returns the current and old-policy velocities of one query with one JJ, so the estimate of (iii) is shared by construction; VInd adds the correction Equation (87), ReplayVInd uses Equation (109), VInd(cd=False) drops JJ where it cancels (Appendix C), and VAux adds vϕv_{\phi} and fits it once per outer iteration by Equation (88).

(iv) The loss weights. Equation (28) leaves three per-sample, detached weights free,

(Wreg,Wrwd,ω),\big(W_{\mathrm{reg}},\ W_{\mathrm{rwd}},\ \omega\big), (89)

namely the weight of the self-regression term, the weight of the reward-augmentation term, and the signed reward coefficient of the reward step. The four families differ mainly in these weights, which are given in Equation (97), Equation (103), Equation (106) and Equation (107) and returned, with the sign of ω\omega, by the hook weights.

Stage 4: the decoupled two-term loss

This stage implements Equation (30) without the group index and with the norms replaced by the per-sample mean meansp⁡[⋅]\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\cdot\right] of Appendix A, which is the reduction used in the code. Given (x~θ,x~reg,x~base,x~rwd,Wreg,Wrwd,ω)\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta};\ \tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}},\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}},\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}};\ W_{\mathrm{reg}},W_{\mathrm{rwd}},\omega\big), every trainer except FewStepOPSD, which adds a second reward square (§5.6), minimises

ℒ=Wreg​meansp​[(x~θ−x~reg)2]⏟ℒreg​(self-regression)+Wrwd​meansp​[(x~θ−sg⁡(x~θ+g))2]⏟ℒrwd​(reward augmentation),{\;\mathcal{L}\;=\;\underbrace{W_{\mathrm{reg}}\,\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}\big)^{2}\right]}_{\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}\ \text{(self-regression)}}\;+\;\underbrace{W_{\mathrm{rwd}}\,\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}+g)\big)^{2}\right]}_{\textstyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}}\ \text{(reward augmentation)}},\;} (90)

with the reward displacement

g=ω⁡(x~rwd−x~base)(detached).g\;=\;\omega\big(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}\big)\qquad\text{(detached).} (91)

With a single reward term, the base interface is specified by six entries:

(x~reg,x~base,x~rwd,Wreg,Wrwd,ω).\big(\ \tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}},\ \tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}},\ \tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}},\ W_{\mathrm{reg}},\ W_{\mathrm{rwd}},\ \omega\ \big).

§§5.3–5.6 specify these quantities, one family at a time, from the derivations of Examples 6–9; FewStepOPSD provides branch-indexed (x~rwd,k,ωk)(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd},k},\omega_{k}) entries. Setting x~reg=∅\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\varnothing switches off ℒreg\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}; setting x~base=∅\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\varnothing switches off ℒrwd\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}}.

Section 5.2 implements Stage 4 except the velocity penalty. The ∅\varnothing cases correspond to the two None checks, so every trainer except FewStepOPSD and ReFL runs the same loss regardless of the anchors it defines.

In addition to Equation (90), an implemented loss may include a velocity penalty against a frozen reference with its own weight, which encourages the policy to stay close to the reference. This penalty is a separate term and not an additional anchor. The average-velocity reference urefu_{\mathrm{ref}} is the initial pre-RL policy and remains fixed throughout training. For an endpoint-renoise query the KL-u penalty is

ℒKLu=meansp⁡[(uθ​(x~t,t,r)−uref​(x~t,t,r))2].\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{u}}_{\mathrm{KL}}=\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\big(u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)-u_{\mathrm{ref}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)\big)^{2}\right]. (92)

When the reference is an instantaneous velocity, here the teacher vrealv_{\mathrm{real}}, it cannot be compared with uθu_{\theta} directly for r≠tr\neq t. We therefore convert it to an average-velocity target as in MeanFlow and regress uθu_{\theta} onto it (the KL-v penalty),

ℒKLv=meansp⁡[(uθ​(x~t,t,r)−(vreal​(x~t,t)−J⁡[uold,t,r]))2].\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{KL}}=\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\Big(u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)-\big(v_{\mathrm{real}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t)-J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big]\big)\Big)^{2}\right]. (93)

5.3 FewStepGRPO: Replaying Stored Trajectories

FewStepGRPO is our replay-based surrogate adaptation of FlowGRPO (Liu et al., 2025a).

Stochastic sampler.

The stochastic sampler generalises Equation (11). Each step first moves from tjt_{j} to a level sj≤tj+1s_{j}\leq t_{j+1}, drawn uniformly from the remaining grid levels, and then adds noise to return to level tj+1t_{j+1} on the linear path,

x^sj=X⁡[x^tj,uold​(x^tj,tj,sj),sj],x^tj+1=1−tj+11−sj​x^sj+τj​ϵ′,ϵ′∼𝒩⁡(0,I),\hat{x}_{s_{j}}=X\big[\hat{x}_{t_{j}},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\hat{x}_{t_{j}},t_{j},s_{j}),\,s_{j}\big],\qquad\hat{x}_{t_{j+1}}=\frac{1-t_{j+1}}{1-s_{j}}\,\hat{x}_{s_{j}}+\tau_{j}\,\epsilon^{\prime},\qquad\epsilon^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), (94)

where the leading coefficient matches the clean component at level tj+1t_{j+1} and τj\tau_{j} matches the noise variance, τj2=tj+12−(1−tj+11−sj)2​sj2\tau_{j}^{2}=t_{j+1}^{2}-\big(\tfrac{1-t_{j+1}}{1-s_{j}}\big)^{2}s_{j}^{2}, which is non-negative if and only if sj≤tj+1s_{j}\leq t_{j+1}. In Equation (94), sjs_{j} is the level at which the flow map is queried and tj+1t_{j+1} is the target level of the step; in the notation of Equation (5), the flow map is thus queried with lower endpoint sjs_{j} rather than r=tj+1r=t_{j+1}, and r=tj+1r=t_{j+1} denotes the target level of the transition. Equation (11) is the case sj=0s_{j}=0, with t′t^{\prime} in place of tj+1t_{j+1}.

Replay-trajectory query.

Unlike endpoint-renoise trainers, it retains the MstepM_{\mathrm{step}} transitions of the stochastic rollout, replays one stored (xt,xr,t,r)(x_{t},x_{r},t,r) per inner iteration, and redraws only the flow-map query level ss, with the law of rr in Stage 3 (i). The redrawn ss need not equal the grid level sjs_{j} used at rollout time; Section B.2 shows that the scored kernel is unaffected by this choice at zero drift. Thus nit=Mstepn_{\mathrm{it}}=M_{\mathrm{step}}, one endpoint advantage supervises all transitions of a member, and the differentiated quantity is the mean μθ\mu_{\theta} of the scoring kernel at level rr instead of a clean prediction.

Scoring kernel.

FewStepGRPO scores xrx_{r} with an Euler–Maruyama Gaussian, which reads

μθ\displaystyle\mu_{\theta} :=αt​xt−bt​(uθ​(xt,t,s)+J),\displaystyle:=\alpha_{t}\,x_{t}-b_{t}\,\big(u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)+J\big), (95)
μold\displaystyle\mu_{\mathrm{old}} :=αt​xt−bt​(uold​(xt,t,s)+J),\displaystyle:=\alpha_{t}\,x_{t}-b_{t}\,\big(u_{\mathrm{old}}(x_{t},t,s)+J\big),
αt\displaystyle\alpha_{t} :=1−ςt22​tΔt,bt:=(1+ςt2​(1−t)2​t)Δt,σk:=ςtΔ​t.\displaystyle:=1-\frac{\varsigma_{t}^{2}}{2t}\,\Delta t,\qquad b_{t}:=\Big(1+\frac{\varsigma_{t}^{2}(1-t)}{2t}\Big)\Delta t,\qquad\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}:=\varsigma_{t}\sqrt{\Delta t}.

Here Δ​t=t−r\Delta t=t-r, αt\alpha_{t} and btb_{t} are the Euler–Maruyama coefficients, σk\sigma_{\mathrm{k}} is the kernel width, ςt\varsigma_{t} is the noise scale of the scoring kernel, and both means use the same detached correction J=J⁡[uold,t,s]J=J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,s\big] evaluated on the replay trajectory with lower endpoint ss. The definition of ςt\varsigma_{t} that avoids the singularity at t0=1t_{0}=1, the trajectory correction and the SDE derivation are deferred to Section B.2.

Anchors and weights.

The tempered (per-element-averaged) scoring ratio and its detached clipping gate are, explicitly,

ρ¯GRPO\displaystyle\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}} :=exp⁡[meansp⁡[(μold−xr)2]−meansp⁡[(μθ−xr)2]2​σk2],\displaystyle:=\exp\!\left[\frac{\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[(\mu_{\mathrm{old}}-x_{r})^{2}\right]-\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[(\mu_{\theta}-x_{r})^{2}\right]}{2\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}}\right], (96)
χGRPO\displaystyle\chi_{\mathrm{GRPO}} :=[(A>0∧ρ¯GRPO≤1+εclip)∨(A<0∧ρ¯GRPO≥1−εclip)].\displaystyle:=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\big(A>0\ \wedge\ \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}\leq 1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}\big)\ \vee\ \big(A<0\ \wedge\ \bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}\geq 1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}\big)\right].

Thus χGRPO=0\chi_{\mathrm{GRPO}}=0 when A=0A=0. The quantity ρ¯GRPO\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}} is a surrogate scoring ratio rather than a rollout importance weight. The anchors and weights are

x~θ\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\theta} =μθ,x~reg=∅,x~base=sg(μθ),x~rwd=xr,\displaystyle=\mu_{\theta},\qquad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\varnothing,\qquad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\operatorname{sg}(\mu_{\theta}),\qquad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}=x_{r}, (97)
Wreg\displaystyle W_{\mathrm{reg}} =0,Wrwd=W=ρ¯GRPO,ω=χGRPO​A2​σk2,\displaystyle=0,\qquad W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=W=\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}},\qquad\omega=\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{GRPO}}\,A}{2\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}},

so only μθ\mu_{\theta} is differentiated. Sections B.2 and B.3 give the tempered interpretation and show that Equation (90) reproduces its clipped gradient. An auxiliary (v-aux) variant is not used because vϕv_{\phi} is fitted on endpoint-renoised states rather than replayed sampler states (Section B.1).

5.4 FewStepAWM: MeanFlowAWM and DMDAWM

FewStepAWM adapts Equation (17) as one clipped reward-augmentation term on the matching residual of the model. It has no explicit self-regression term, and in MeanFlowAWM the reward displacement is measured from the detached current prediction.

Rollout and prediction.

Stage 1 uses the deterministic rollout, nit=ntsn_{\mathrm{it}}=n_{\mathrm{ts}}, and every inner iteration draws a fresh (t,r,ϵ)(t,r,\epsilon), re-noises the rewarded endpoint and computes the v-prediction Equation (86),

x~t=AddNoise​(x^,t),x~θ=x~θ,v=X⁡[x~t,uθ​(x~t,t,r)+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0],\tilde{x}_{t}=\textsc{AddNoise}(\hat{x},t),\qquad\tilde{x}_{\theta}=\tilde{x}_{\theta,\mathrm{v}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big], (98)

so that, by Equation (22),

x~θ−x^=−t⁡(uθ−(vcond−J⁡[uold,t,r])),vcond=ϵ−x^.\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\hat{x}=-t\Big(u_{\theta}-\big(v_{\mathrm{cond}}-J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big]\big)\Big),\qquad v_{\mathrm{cond}}=\epsilon-\hat{x}. (99)

Thus uθu_{\theta} regresses onto vcond−Jv_{\mathrm{cond}}-J, the MeanFlow target Equation (8) with the conditional velocity in place of the teacher.

MeanFlowAWM anchors and weights.

The method uses the rollout endpoint as the rewarded anchor, no explicit self-regression, and the current prediction as baseline: x~rwd=x^\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\hat{x}, x~reg=∅\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\varnothing, x~base=sg⁡(x~θ)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}). Besides the shared JJ in x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta}, the old policy enters only through the weights, via the shared-JJ prediction of Stage 3 (iii),

x~ind=X⁡[x~t,uold​(x~t,t,r)+J⁡[uold,t,r], 0],x~θ−x~ind=−t⁡(uθ−uold).\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)+J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big],\,0\big],\qquad\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}=-t\big(u_{\theta}-u_{\mathrm{old}}\big). (100)

The weights reuse the quadratic-exponential form of §5.3, but not its probabilistic interpretation:

ρAWM\displaystyle\rho_{\mathrm{AWM}} :=exp⁡[meansp⁡[(x~ind−x^)2]−meansp⁡[(x~θ−x^)2]2​τAWM2],\displaystyle:=\exp\!\left[\frac{\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[(\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}-\hat{x})^{2}\right]-\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[(\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\hat{x})^{2}\right]}{2\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}^{2}}\right], (101)
χAWM\displaystyle\chi_{\mathrm{AWM}} :=[(A>0∧ρAWM≤1+εclip)∨(A<0∧ρAWM≥1−εclip)].\displaystyle:=\mathbf{1}\!\left[\big(A>0\ \wedge\ \rho_{\mathrm{AWM}}\leq 1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}\big)\ \vee\ \big(A<0\ \wedge\ \rho_{\mathrm{AWM}}\geq 1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}\big)\right].

Thus χAWM=0\chi_{\mathrm{AWM}}=0 when A=0A=0. The implemented residual scale is τAWM=max⁡{t,τmin}\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}=\max\{t,\tau_{\min}\}; unlike in FewStepGRPO, no sampler kernel determines this scale. The choice τAWM=t\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}=t would cancel the factor t2t^{2} in both residuals; when the floor is active, the factor t2/τAWM2t^{2}/\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}^{2} remains:

∂ℒ∂uθ=ρAWM​χAWM​AN​t2τAWM2​(uθ−(vcond−J⁡[uold,t,r]))\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial u_{\theta}}=\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{AWM}}\,\chi_{\mathrm{AWM}}\,A}{N}\frac{t^{2}}{\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}^{2}}\Big(u_{\theta}-\big(v_{\mathrm{cond}}-J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big]\big)\Big) (102)

and its factor t2/τAWM2t^{2}/\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}^{2} equals one only above the floor. The resulting quantities are

x~reg=∅,x~base=sg⁡(x~θ),x~rwd=x^,Wreg=0,Wrwd=W=ρAWM,ω=χAWM​A2​τAWM2.\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\varnothing,\quad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}),\quad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\hat{x},\quad W_{\mathrm{reg}}=0,\quad W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=W=\rho_{\mathrm{AWM}},\quad\omega=\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{AWM}}\,A}{2\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}^{2}}. (103)

Relative to Equation (32) with w⁡(t)=1w(t)=1, the step has an extra factor 12\tfrac{1}{2}, which comes from the Gaussian form of the statistic and is absorbed by the learning rate. ρAWM\rho_{\mathrm{AWM}} is not an importance weight, since (x~t,x^)(\tilde{x}_{t},\hat{x}) is not a transition of the rollout; through the gate χAWM\chi_{\mathrm{AWM}}, it limits one-sided changes of the matching residual relative to uoldu_{\mathrm{old}}. We call this variant MeanFlowAWM.

DMDAWM variant.

The reported v-aux variant, DMDAWM, drops JJ in the current and old-policy predictions (the JJ-free (t,r)(t,r) query and x~ind|J=0{\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}|_{J=0}} of §4.3) and replaces the reward baseline with the prediction of the auxiliary network:

x~θ=X[x~t,uθ(x~t,t,r), 0],x~ind|J=0=X[x~t,uold(x~t,t,r), 0],x~base=x~aux,ρAWM=exp⁡[meansp⁡[(x~ind|J=0−x^)2]−meansp⁡[(x~θ−x^)2]2​τAWM2],∂ℒ∂uθ=ρAWM​χAWM​AN​t2τAWM2​(vϕ−vcond).\begin{gathered}\tilde{x}_{\theta}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big],\qquad{\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}|_{J=0}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big],\qquad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}},\\ \rho_{\mathrm{AWM}}=\exp\!\left[\frac{\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[({\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}|_{J=0}}-\hat{x})^{2}\right]-\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[(\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\hat{x})^{2}\right]}{2\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}^{2}}\right],\\ \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial u_{\theta}}=\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{AWM}}\,\chi_{\mathrm{AWM}}\,A}{N}\frac{t^{2}}{\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}^{2}}\big(v_{\phi}-v_{\mathrm{cond}}\big).\end{gathered} (104)

Above the floor the factor t2/τAWM2t^{2}/\tau_{\mathrm{AWM}}^{2} equals one; descent moves uθu_{\theta} along +A⁡(vcond−vϕ)+A(v_{\mathrm{cond}}-v_{\phi}), with vϕv_{\phi} as a learned per-sample baseline. If a detached JJ were kept in the first two predictions, it would change only the scalar ratio ρAWM\rho_{\mathrm{AWM}} and the clipping gate, but not the gradient direction. The reported method omits it, so it requires no directional-difference evaluation of JJ.

Decoupled loss.

Both variants use Equation (90) with Wreg=0W_{\mathrm{reg}}=0, so only ℒrwd\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}} remains. MeanFlowAWM measures the reward displacement from sg⁡(x~θ)\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}); DMDAWM measures it from the auxiliary prediction x~aux\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}}. In code, FewStepAWM implements anchors and weights, and MeanFlowAWM and DMDAWM differ only in their estimator (Section 5.4).

5.5 FewStepNFT: MeanFlowNFT and DMDNFT

FewStepNFT maps the two implicit branches of DiffusionNFT to the two terms of Equation (90). It contains both a self-regression term and a signed reward-augmentation term, with x~rwd=x^\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\hat{x} in both variants.

Anchors, predictions and weights.

For the two variants, the quantities of Equation (35) are listed in Table 3.

The theoretical weights of Equation (35) are modified in the implementation, following its official implementation in (Zheng et al., 2026a). The derivation of §4.2 gives Wreg=Wrwd=β2/t2W_{\mathrm{reg}}=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=\beta^{2}/t^{2} and ω=clip⁡(A,−1,1)/β\omega=\operatorname{clip}(A,-1,1)/\beta, i.e. one fixed per-tt scale for both branches, with r^\hat{r} from Equation (18) and AA normalised within the group. The implementation keeps the two branches but changes the following: the per-tt scale is replaced by one adaptive normaliser per branch, γ±\gamma_{\pm}, the mean absolute residual of that branch; r^\hat{r} is the compressed weight Equation (84) with clip range cadvc_{\mathrm{adv}}; and AA is the advantage Equation (83). The weights are then

γ±=max⁡{meansp⁡[|x~base±β⁡(sg⁡(x~θ)−x~reg)−x^|],εγ},a+=r^γ+,a−=1−r^γ−,\gamma_{\pm}=\max\Big\{\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\big|\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}\pm\beta\big(\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta})-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}\big)-\hat{x}\big|\right],\ \varepsilon_{\gamma}\Big\},\quad a_{+}=\frac{\hat{r}}{\gamma_{+}},\quad a_{-}=\frac{1-\hat{r}}{\gamma_{-}}, (105)
Wreg=Wrwd=W=cadv​β2​(a++a−),ω=a+−a−β⁡(a++a−).W_{\mathrm{reg}}=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=W=c_{\mathrm{adv}}\beta^{2}(a_{+}+a_{-}),\qquad\omega=\frac{a_{+}-a_{-}}{\beta\,(a_{+}+a_{-})}. (106)

If γ+=γ−=t2\gamma_{+}=\gamma_{-}=t^{2}, cadv=1c_{\mathrm{adv}}=1 and AA is the group-normalised advantage Equation (12), they reduce to Equation (35), with W=β2/t2W=\beta^{2}/t^{2} and ω=clip⁡(A,−1,1)/β\omega=\operatorname{clip}(A,-1,1)/\beta. In the implemented weighting, r^\hat{r} enters through a±a_{\pm} as a mixing weight, cadvc_{\mathrm{adv}} scales both loss terms to undo the compression of the advantage by 1/(2​cadv)1/(2c_{\mathrm{adv}}) in Equation (84), so that the effective step does not shrink when the clip range is widened (Section B.3), and ω\omega is defined directly. The v-ind estimator gives MeanFlowNFT, and the v-aux estimator gives DMDNFT.

Decoupled loss.

Both variants minimise ℒreg+ℒrwd\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}} with the common weight WW, the rollout endpoint as x~rwd\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd}}, and Table 3 defining x~reg\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}} and x~base\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}.

5.6 FewStepOPSD: Extended Reward Augmentation and ReFL

FewStepOPSD belongs to the family of reward-gradient-based methods (Xu et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026) and is related to gradient-guided distribution matching (Dong et al., 2026). It implements Example 8 (iii) as a FewStepNFT trainer whose rewarded points are constructed from the reward gradient instead of sampled; it therefore uses the normalisers of Equation (105), and its configuration with a single ascent step is the ReFL proxy of Example 9. It modifies more stages than FewStepNFT. Stage 1 depends on the reward, the rewarded anchors are constructed points instead of rollout samples, and Stage 4 overrides loss. Stage 2 is unchanged, and r^\hat{r} enters only through the weights.

Rollout.

FewStepOPSD uses the reward-coupled rollout Equation (82). It first draws the i.i.d. base samples with Equation (81). The reward-coupled construction then applies Equation (62), taking MtgtM_{\mathrm{tgt}} normalised reward-gradient steps in each direction from the r=0r=0 prediction x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}, with the displacement transferred to the anchor by Equation (70), giving x~±\tilde{x}_{\pm}. The points x~±\tilde{x}_{\pm} are detached, so the computation graph of the reward ends here and the policy update does not back-propagate through the decoder or the reward model; the reward must be differentiable.

Anchors and weights.

(i) Query. Each member is queried at a single level tt, drawn from the law given in §6.1; hence nit=1n_{\mathrm{it}}=1. As in Example 8 and Example 9, the query state is the re-noised endpoint x~t=AddNoise​(x^,t)\tilde{x}_{t}=\textsc{AddNoise}(\hat{x},t), so the anchor is evaluated at the same state as the current prediction. The drawn rr is stored and reused at fitting time, so the current prediction and the anchor are queried at the same (t,r)(t,r).

(ii) Anchors. The u-form uses x~reg=x~base=x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}} and the v-form uses x~reg=x~base=x~ind\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}, Equation (69); in both, the rewarded anchors are x~±\tilde{x}_{\pm}. For the v-form, the gradient steps start from the r=0r=0 prediction x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}, which does not depend on JJ, and only the resulting displacement is added to the anchor x~ind\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}} by Equation (70).

(iii) Instantaneous velocity. The v-form uses the shared JJ of Stage 3 (iii). Because both rewarded points are constructed from the anchor, JJ cancels in every difference in the loss, as in Equation (71) and Equation (72). The v-form reported in §6 drops JJ and evaluates no directional difference (Equation (87)); in code its estimator is VInd(cd=False).

(iv) Weights. With Equation (105) evaluated at x~±\tilde{x}_{\pm},

Wreg=Wrwd=W\displaystyle W_{\mathrm{reg}}=W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=W =cadv​β2​(a++a−),\displaystyle=c_{\mathrm{adv}}\beta^{2}(a_{+}+a_{-}), (107)
ω1=a+β⁡(a++a−),ω2\displaystyle\omega_{1}=\frac{a_{+}}{\beta\,(a_{+}+a_{-})},\quad\omega_{2} =−a−β⁡(a++a−),|ω1|+|ω2|=1β,\displaystyle=-\frac{a_{-}}{\beta\,(a_{+}+a_{-})},\qquad|\omega_{1}|+|\omega_{2}|=\frac{1}{\beta},

so the sum of coefficient magnitudes is fixed at 1/β1/\beta and r^\hat{r} redistributes it between the two terms. It can still change the common weight WW when γ+≠γ−\gamma_{+}\neq\gamma_{-}. The factor cadvc_{\mathrm{adv}} scales the common weight but not the split between the branches.

Decoupled loss.

The loss Equation (68) consists of one self-regression term and two reward-augmentation terms, which share the baseline and differ in the rewarded point x~rwd,k\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{rwd},k} and the coefficient ωk\omega_{k}; the signs of ωk\omega_{k} are fixed by construction and do not depend on AA.

ReFL.

The ReFL configuration of Equation (68), identified in Example 9, reuses the stages above, with the changes below. Stage 1 takes a single ascent step, Mtgt=1M_{\mathrm{tgt}}=1, without a descent point. As for FewStepOPSD, the step starts at the r=0r=0 prediction and its displacement is added back by Equation (70), so ∇R\nabla R is evaluated at x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}} as specified by Equation (78). Stage 2 is not used, because ReFL has no advantage; ω1>0\omega_{1}>0 is fixed by construction and the implementation sets r^≡1\hat{r}\equiv 1 in Equation (107), giving ω1=1/β\omega_{1}=1/\beta and Wrwd=cadv​β2/γ+W_{\mathrm{rwd}}=c_{\mathrm{adv}}\beta^{2}/\gamma_{+}, detached and positive as Example 9 allows. The ReFL override keeps the factor cadvc_{\mathrm{adv}} of Equation (107). Stage 3 keeps the same anchors. Stage 4 keeps only ℒrwd,1\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd},1} with Wreg=0W_{\mathrm{reg}}=0, i.e. the loss of Section 5.6 reduces to its ascent term (Section 5.6). The resulting gradient is that of Equation (79), the few-step form of Equation (77).

5.7 Cost of an Outer Iteration

Table 4 lists the network evaluations per inner iteration for each network. The rollout of Stage 1 is amortised over one outer iteration and is not counted here. Each entry is determined by the family and the estimator of §5.1: nitn_{\mathrm{it}} by queries, cJc_{J} by the estimator (22 for the directional-difference estimate of v-ind, and 00 otherwise), and cϕc_{\phi} and the auxiliary part of cextrac_{\mathrm{extra}} by v-aux; the reward-coupled construction of FewStepOPSD and ReFL is counted in cextrac_{\mathrm{extra}}. The counters cθc_{\theta}, coldc_{\mathrm{old}}, cJc_{J}, cϕc_{\phi}, crefc_{\mathrm{ref}}, cextrac_{\mathrm{extra}}, CC and CrolloutC_{\mathrm{rollout}} are defined in the caption and listed in Appendix A.

6 Experiment

Having established a general view of these methods, we use experiments to answer three questions. Every trainer of §§5.3–5.6 implements one of these methods, minimises the same loss form, and differs mainly in its anchors and weights. (i) Which of these choices, in particular the reward signal and the estimator of the instantaneous velocity, determine how effectively and how efficiently a few-step generator is fine-tuned, and how strongly it exploits the reward? (ii) Do these conclusions carry over to a different modality, or do they show limitations in other scenarios? (iii) Does a generator fine-tuned at a few steps improve when it is sampled with more steps, without retraining?

6.1 Setup on Image Generation

Generator and sampler.

The policy is the average-velocity network uθ​(x~t,t,r)u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r) of §3, initialised from the pretrained SD3.5-Medium backbone (Stability AI, 2024; Esser et al., 2024) and distilled with AnyFlow (Gu et al., 2026), which first trains with the MeanFlow identity Equation (6) and then applies on-policy distribution matching Equation (10) against the frozen teacher. Reinforcement learning trains a LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) of rank 3232 (scaling 6464) on the attention projections, at resolution 512×512512\times 512. We set Mstep=4M_{\mathrm{step}}=4 steps on the grid of levels {1,0.9,0.75,0.5,0}\{1,0.9,0.75,0.5,0\}, without classifier-free guidance (Ho and Salimans, 2021), with the deterministic sampler of Equation (5) for every trainer except FewStepGRPO, which requires the stochastic sampler of Equation (94). Evaluation always uses the deterministic sampler on the same grid.

Optimisation.

In Stage 1 and Stage 2, each outer iteration draws 4848 prompts with K=24K=24 members each, i.e. 11521152 rollouts, on 88 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. All methods use AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with learning rate 3×10−63\times 10^{-6}, weight decay 10−410^{-4} and gradient-norm clipping at 11; an old policy uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} given by an EMA of uθu_{\theta}, refreshed once per outer iteration after the policy update with the decay schedule of the official DiffusionNFT implementation (Section D.1); for the NFT/OPSD families, β=0.1\beta=0.1 and cadv=5c_{\mathrm{adv}}=5 in Equation (84); and the KL-u penalty against the fixed AnyFlow initial policy, using Equation (92) with weight 10−410^{-4}. An ablation with the penalty Equation (93), labelled KL-v, on MeanFlowNFT is given in Section D.4. Stage 3 (i) draws tt and rr as the maximum and the minimum of two uniforms before the time shift of the SD3 scheduler, t↦3​t/(1+2​t)t\mapsto 3t/(1+2t) (shift 3.03.0, the same shifted grid as in sampling), sets half of each batch to r=tr=t and a quarter to r=0r=0, and uses nts=4n_{\mathrm{ts}}=4 queries per member and outer iteration. The floors are τmin=10−2\tau_{\min}=10^{-2}, εγ=10−5\varepsilon_{\gamma}=10^{-5}, εg=10−12\varepsilon_{g}=10^{-12} and εstd=10−4\varepsilon_{\mathrm{std}}=10^{-4}, and εcd=5×10−3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}}=5\times 10^{-3} (Section D.1).

Rewards.

We use two reward settings to test the methods. The first is the OCR setting, where the reward is the OCR accuracy of the text rendered in the image with the OCR prompts. It has no gradient with respect to the clean sample, so FewStepOPSD and ReFL, which require ∇R\nabla R, do not apply. In the mixed-reward setting the reward is the unweighted sum of CLIPScore, HPSv2 and PickScore on the PickScore prompt set (Hessel et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2023; Kirstain et al., 2023).

Specific settings.

For the group-advantage-based methods, nit=4n_{\mathrm{it}}=4, with nit=Mstepn_{\mathrm{it}}=M_{\mathrm{step}} for FewStepGRPO and nit=ntsn_{\mathrm{it}}=n_{\mathrm{ts}} for the others. FewStepGRPO retains the states of Equation (94) and uses the base noise scale ς=0.25\varsigma=0.25 of ςt\varsigma_{t} in Equation (95) (Equation (110)), with clipping radius εclip=4×10−3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}=4\times 10^{-3} (OCR) or 3×10−33\times 10^{-3} (mixed reward) in χGRPO\chi_{\mathrm{GRPO}}; MeanFlowAWM and DMDAWM use radius 10−210^{-2} (OCR) or 2×10−32\times 10^{-3} (mixed reward) in χAWM\chi_{\mathrm{AWM}}. For DMDAWM and DMDNFT, the auxiliary velocity vϕv_{\phi} is fitted by Equation (88) with learning rate 10−510^{-5} and nfm=5n_{\mathrm{fm}}=5 steps per outer iteration. FewStepOPSD uses κ=0.1\kappa=0.1, Mtgt=2M_{\mathrm{tgt}}=2 and η=1\eta=1 in Equation (62), with ∇R\nabla R of the full training reward, drawing tt from a logit-normal law with median 0.2780.278 (5–95% range [0.125,0.508][0.125,0.508]), i.e., the small noise levels of Example 8, and rr as in Stage 3 (i). ReFL is Example 9 with Mtgt=1M_{\mathrm{tgt}}=1, r^≡1\hat{r}\equiv 1 and ∇R\nabla R of the full training reward; for a fair comparison, uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} is also the EMA of uθu_{\theta}. A summary of the methods is given in Table 5.

Baselines.

In the mixed-reward setting we additionally run the original objectives on the pre-RL few-step model without the adaptation of §4.3, i.e., with the average velocity uθ​(x~t,t,r)u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r), rr drawn as in Stage 3 (i) (ss for FlowGRPO), substituted for the instantaneous velocity wherever the original objective requires one. For DiffusionNFT and AWM, it is Equation (47) with uθ​(x~t,t,r)u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r) in place of uθ​(x~t,t,0)u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,0). For FlowGRPO, this substitution is not theoretically solid. We denote these baselines by the names of the original methods, FlowGRPO, AWM and DiffusionNFT, and compare them with FewStepGRPO, MeanFlowAWM and MeanFlowNFT, respectively, while keeping the other setting the same. In addition, by Appendix C, the detached correction JJ cancels from its v-form loss, so the u-form in the FewStepOPSD family is the special case of the v-form in which rr is fixed to 00 instead of being drawn at every query, so we did not compare them.

Evaluation.

Three sources are used, with the conventions of the figures. (i) Online, every 5050 iterations, within training: the aesthetic score, CLIPScore and OCR accuracy, and in the mixed-reward setting HPSv2 and PickScore; on DrawBench prompts (Saharia et al., 2022) in the mixed-reward setting, and on the OCR prompt set for OCR accuracy and for every dimension of the OCR setting. (ii) Offline, at the checkpoints saved every 100100 iterations, on 256256 images with seed 1234512345 and the same prompts: HPSv3 and ImageReward (Ma et al., 2025b; Xu et al., 2023). (iii) Offline, GenEval2 (Soft-TIFA) (Kamath et al., 2025), the successor to GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023), in its official evaluation setting, following MeanFlowNFT (Huang et al., 2026b) (Section D.1). The LAION aesthetic score (Schuhmann, 2022), HPSv3, ImageReward and GenEval2 serve as held-out evaluators, as do OCR accuracy in the mixed-reward setting and CLIPScore in the OCR setting. Iteration 00 is the shared AnyFlow Init. checkpoint.

6.2 Setup on Video Generation

Generator and sampler.

The policy is the few-step generator of §3 on the Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B backbone (Team Wan et al., 2025), distilled on-policy with AnyFlow (Gu et al., 2026) against its frozen teacher as in the image setting. Reinforcement learning trains a LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) of rank 3232 (scaling 6464) on the attention projections, at 480×832480\times 832 and 8181 frames, i.e. latents of shape 21×16×60×10421\times 16\times 60\times 104. We set Mstep=4M_{\mathrm{step}}=4 steps without classifier-free guidance (Ho and Salimans, 2021), with the deterministic sampler of Equation (5) for every method except FewStepGRPO, which requires Equation (94). Evaluation always uses the deterministic sampler.

Optimisation.

Each outer iteration draws two batches, each with 22 prompts per rank and K=16K=16 members, on 3232 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, i.e. 20482048 rollouts per outer iteration. We use AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) with learning rate 3×10−63\times 10^{-6} and gradient-norm clipping at 11; uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} is an EMA of uθu_{\theta} refreshed once per outer iteration; for the NFT/OPSD families, β=0.1\beta=0.1 and cadv=5c_{\mathrm{adv}}=5 in Equation (84); the KL-u penalty against the fixed AnyFlow initial policy uses Equation (92) with weight 10−410^{-4}; and each member is queried nts=4n_{\mathrm{ts}}=4 times, with half of each batch set to r=tr=t and a quarter to r=0r=0. For FewStepOPSD and ReFL, the world size is 4848 instead, because computing the gradient with respect to the video latents requires much memory, while the per-rank batch is unchanged. FewStepOPSD and ReFL therefore use 30723072 rollouts per outer iteration, 1.51.5 times as many as the 32-GPU runs. The runs are thus matched in the number of outer iterations but not in the number of samples, and the quality comparison should be interpreted with this caveat. GPU-hours remain comparable across runs, whereas s/iter is reported but is not comparable across runs with different world sizes.

Rewards.

Using the same four reward components as the LongCat/MeanFlowNFT video setup (Meituan LongCat Team et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026b), we define our training reward as an unweighted sum. The HPSv3 scorer (Ma et al., 2025b) enters through HPSv3-general and HPSv3-percentile (per-frame, the latter the mean of the top 30%30\% of frames under the caption); VideoAlign’s motion quality (MQ) and text alignment (TA) are drawn from video-feedback scoring (Liu et al., 2025b). MQ and TA are zz-normalised before entering the sum; tables report their raw scorer outputs. Only HPSv3 is differentiable here, and its two reductions account for 96%96\% of the aggregate reward under the zz-normalised weights (Section D.5). The VideoAlign reward takes file paths as input and decodes the videos in its own pipeline, so there is no differentiable path from the latents to this reward. FewStepOPSD and ReFL therefore use only the gradients of the HPSv3 terms, while they are evaluated on all four terms; Section D.5 quantifies this asymmetry, which does not occur in the image setting.

Specific settings.

As in the image setting, nit=4n_{\mathrm{it}}=4 for the group-advantage-based methods (nit=Mstepn_{\mathrm{it}}=M_{\mathrm{step}} for FewStepGRPO, nit=ntsn_{\mathrm{it}}=n_{\mathrm{ts}} for the others), and the auxiliary velocity vϕv_{\phi} is fitted by Equation (88) with learning rate 10−510^{-5} and nfm=5n_{\mathrm{fm}}=5 steps per outer iteration for DMDAWM and DMDNFT. Because there is one reward setting rather than two, the gate radius εclip=10−3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}}=10^{-3} is used for both χGRPO\chi_{\mathrm{GRPO}} in FewStepGRPO and χAWM\chi_{\mathrm{AWM}} in MeanFlowAWM/DMDAWM, and FewStepGRPO uses ς=0.7\varsigma=0.7 in Equation (95). FewStepOPSD and ReFL require further settings, because the video backbone imposes three constraints on ∇R\nabla R that do not occur in the image setting. First, as stated above, ∇R\nabla R is computed from the two HPSv3 reductions instead of the full training reward; the VideoAlign terms still enter the reward and the advantage but do not contribute to the gradient. Second, the reward model is cast to fp32 with the sdpa attention backend; with the released bfloat16 weights, the reward gradient changes direction substantially while the reward value changes by only ∼0.003{\sim}0.003, and since Equation (62) normalises ∇R\nabla R to unit length and thus uses only its direction, this error directly affects the update. Third, the video is decoded one latent frame at a time, so ∇R\nabla R is computed from 2121 of the 8181 pixel frames of a clip, each decoded without its causal prefix; Section D.5 reports the memory measurements that make this necessary.

Evaluation.

We use two evaluations that measure different properties. (i) Every 1010 iterations, we compute the four training rewards on 256256 held-out prompts with seed 1234512345. Since this is the training objective, it cannot distinguish a quality gain from reward hacking. (ii) At iteration 250250, we evaluate VBench (Huang et al., 2024) on 946946 GPT-augmented prompts × 5\times\,5 samples =4730=4730 videos per method, with all 1616 dimensions aggregated by the quality/semantic/overall weights of AnyFlow (Gu et al., 2026). No method optimises any part of it. Iteration 00 is the shared pre-RL checkpoint trained with AnyFlow.

6.3 Main Results on Image Generation

Effectiveness.

Table 6 and Figures 4 and 4 support the following observations.

  1. (i)

    The adaptation of §4.3 is beneficial in these runs, and the v-prediction form gives better performance in most of these comparisons (Figures 6 and 1). FewStepGRPO raises the training reward from 1.4501.450 to 1.4611.461 and the held-out HPSv3 from 10.3010.30 to 11.5811.58, whereas FlowGRPO, its counterpart with direct employment of average-velocity, leaves the training reward at 1.4381.438 and lowers HPSv3 to 9.629.62. Meanwhile, MeanFlowNFT as the v-prediction counterpart of DiffusionNFT, which is the direct employment of average-velocity, reaches a training reward of 1.5091.509 against 1.4401.440, and is higher on the held-out HPSv3 (13.2313.23 against 11.7911.79), ImageReward (1.3851.385 against 1.3171.317) and best GenEval2 (0.4110.411 against 0.3990.399), the last within the ∼0.03{\sim}0.03 resolution.

  2. (ii)

    In the OCR setting, DMDAWM, MeanFlowNFT and DMDNFT raise OCR accuracy from 0.4980.498 to at least 0.850.85 within 100100–150150 iterations, whereas MeanFlowAWM and FewStepGRPO reach only 0.8020.802 and 0.7760.776 at iteration 200200. Furthermore, it can be observed that within the 200200-iteration horizon of Figure 4, the highest logged OCR accuracy is reached by MeanFlowNFT, about 0.9450.945 at iteration 150150, and it is also the first to reach 0.850.85, at iteration 100100. DMDAWM starts lower at iteration 5050 but rises steeply thereafter and reaches 0.9360.936 at iteration 200200, where the two curves coincide within the resolution of the plot (Table 6a). Its rapid rise is consistent with a combination of two properties. (i) It has no self-regression (x~reg=∅\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\varnothing), so only reward augmentation contributes to its decoupled update. (ii) It is DMD-based and models the instantaneous velocity with the auxiliary network vϕv_{\phi}, which is refitted to the current rollouts at every iteration, so the baseline x~base=x~aux\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}} follows the policy; since this baseline is fixed within an update, reward augmentation uses the direction A⁡(vcond−vϕ)A\,(v_{\mathrm{cond}}-v_{\phi}) instead of one based on the directional-difference estimate Equation (87). This fast increase coincides with the large held-out degradation; at its first checkpoint with OCR accuracy above 0.820.82, HPSv3 drops from 12.8612.86 to 5.055.05 and ImageReward from 1.2331.233 to 0.0920.092.

  3. (iii)

    In the mixed-reward setting, FewStepOPSD and ReFL achieve the two highest training rewards, with FewStepOPSD highest at the final iteration. Using the gradient of the full reward, the two raise the training reward from 1.4501.450 to 1.641.64 and 1.621.62, against 1.461.46–1.521.52 for the five group-advantage methods, and they also lead on ImageReward and GenEval2. Their curves nearly coincide (Figure 4); the logged coefficient magnitudes of FewStepOPSD differ by 0.240.24 between the two branches, i.e. 2.4%2.4\% of their fixed sum 1/β=101/\beta=10, although the two reward-augmentation vectors also depend on their different increments (Section D.3). Among the five group-advantage methods, DMDNFT and MeanFlowNFT come next and perform similarly (training reward 1.511.51–1.521.52, GenEval2 0.410.41 at iteration 400400).

  4. (iv)

    In the default mixed-reward configuration, none of the five group-advantage runs increases CLIPScore, which decreases slightly from 0.2890.289 to 0.2790.279–0.2850.285, whereas FewStepOPSD and ReFL raise it to 0.3170.317–0.3220.322. Dedicated CLIP-focused group-advantage ablations do increase it (Section D.2).

Efficiency.

We measure efficiency by the time per iteration (Table 7) and the time to reach the best checkpoint (Figure 5a). It can be observed that

  1. (i)

    The two reward-gradient-based methods are the cheapest per iteration, 219219 s for ReFL and 268268 s for FewStepOPSD, because they compute one update direction per member in the clean-sample space with one query of uθu_{\theta} instead of four (nit=1n_{\mathrm{it}}=1), and because JJ cancels in their loss. However, their sampling time, which includes the reward-coupled rollout of Equation (82), is 175175–225225 s per iteration, against about 7878 s for the plain rollout of the other five methods (Table 7). Since the reward is defined in pixel space, its gradient with respect to the clean latent requires back-propagation through both the reward model and the VAE decoder.

  2. (ii)

    The directional-difference evaluations Equation (87) and Equation (109) for the shared-JJ v-form plausibly account for most of the cost difference. FewStepGRPO, MeanFlowAWM and MeanFlowNFT require two additional forward passes of uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} per query. These methods take 423423–435435 s, against 304304–326326 s for DMDAWM and DMDNFT, which compute the baseline from vϕv_{\phi} and compute no JJ. The difference arises in the update time (344344–355355 against 223223–245245 s), and the OCR setting gives the same ordering (451451–496496 against 342342–346346 s).

  3. (iii)

    ReFL has a marginally higher best GenEval2 point estimate than FewStepOPSD (0.4650.465 against 0.4630.463), but the 0.0020.002 gap is below the stated 0.030.03 resolution and does not separate the two methods. ReFL reaches its selected checkpoint after 12.212.2 h (iteration 200200), whereas FewStepOPSD continues to iteration 400400 (29.829.8 h); both peak on the held-out aesthetic score and HPSv3 by iteration 100100 (the aesthetic trajectory of FewStepOPSD is tabulated in Table S1; HPSv3 is read from Figure 4), after which these scores decline while the training reward still rises, which is consistent with the onset of reward hacking. Among the group-advantage-based methods, MeanFlowAWM and DMDAWM reach their best GenEval2 early, at iteration 100100 (11.811.8 and 8.48.4 h), but at lower values (0.3970.397 and 0.3770.377).

6.4 Main Results on Video Generation

Effectiveness.

Table 8 and Table S2 support the following observations.

  1. (i)

    FewStepGRPO is the least effective at increasing the training reward. It is the only group-advantage-based method that ends below the shared initialisation (15.8915.89 against 16.5416.54), and its TA drops markedly, from 1.851.85 to 1.231.23. Among the group-advantage-based methods DMDNFT is the most effective, raising the training reward to 17.9317.93 (+1.39+1.39) and leading on three of its four terms. In this run the larger training-reward gain coincides with larger held-out degradation. Against MeanFlowAWM, the highest on VBench overall, DMDNFT is 0.320.32 lower in VBench overall (83.3883.38 against 83.7083.70, last of the seven), 5.565.56 lower in dynamic degree (53.3353.33 against 58.8958.89, the lowest of any method) and 0.160.16 lower in TA (1.681.68 against 1.841.84).

  2. (ii)

    Among the remaining methods, FewStepOPSD and ReFL have the lowest training reward after FewStepGRPO, ending at 16.2616.26 and 16.4616.46, slightly below the initialisation. For video, the reward gradient must be computed for every latent token of a long sequence, through the decoder and the reward model, which requires several numerical simplifications in the reward-gradient-based runs. Their VBench point estimates degrade less than that of DMDNFT in these runs, which does not establish that they protect against reward exploitation. TA rises above the initialisation (1.911.91 and 1.891.89 against 1.851.85), ReFL is second on VBench overall (83.6983.69) and first on quality (85.4085.40), and FewStepOPSD has the highest aesthetic quality, background consistency and appearance style of any method (70.8770.87, 95.6895.68 and 74.5374.53); FewStepOPSD and ReFL have the second- and third-highest dynamic degree (59.4459.44 and 59.1759.17).

Efficiency.

The GPU-hours in Table 8 lead to the following observations.

  1. (i)

    Unlike in the image setting, the DMD-based methods are slower than their MeanFlow counterparts, in both s/iter (821821 against 734734–737737 s) and GPU-hours. With nfm=5n_{\mathrm{fm}}=5, omitting the directional difference saves up to 88 forward passes of uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} without gradient per member (nts=4n_{\mathrm{ts}}=4 queries, two each) but adds 55 forward and backward passes of vϕv_{\phi} per outer iteration. The fit costs about 144144 s per iteration and the net s/iter difference is +84+84–8787 s, so the saved JJ passes account for about 6060 s by difference; the fit dominates, plausibly because backward passes through the larger video model are expensive.

  2. (ii)

    The reward-gradient-based methods lose their cost advantage from the image setting and are the two most expensive in GPU-hours. FewStepOPSD and ReFL have a sampling time of up to 674674 s per iteration (FewStepOPSD), which includes the reward-gradient computation, against ∼291{\sim}291 s for the other methods, and an update time of only 112112 s. The gradient of a video reward with respect to the latent tokens is expensive, plausibly because the latent sequence is much longer than for images and because both the reward model and the decoder are larger than their image counterparts. In addition, MQ and TA are not differentiable (§6.2), which further limits these two methods.

6.5 Test-Time Scaling Analysis

In deployment, a few-step model should ideally support several operating points on the quality–latency trade-off, using its training step count for most requests and more sampling steps when higher quality is required. This motivates training at a small MstepM_{\mathrm{step}} while allowing more solver steps at inference. If quality improves without retraining, the model supports test-time scaling and can trade compute for output quality. Flexible-step generation and inference-time scaling have also been studied for consistency-type models, improved MeanFlow and scalable generators (Kim et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a; Geng et al., 2026; Xie et al., 2025a); our experiment is restricted to the checkpoints and solver grid below.

Setup.

We therefore consider the image generation task, and take the checkpoints trained and evaluated at Mstep=4M_{\mathrm{step}}=4 in §6.1 and sample each at Mstep∈{4,8,16,32}M_{\mathrm{step}}\in\{4,8,16,32\}. We use the checkpoints listed in Table S3. We keep the 256256 DrawBench prompts, seed 1234512345, resolution, deterministic sampler Equation (5), absence of classifier-free guidance, and the time shift 3.03.0 of §6.1 fixed. Increasing MstepM_{\mathrm{step}} only refines the same shifted solver grid; no model is retrained. Thus the experiment isolates a 1×1{\times}, 2×2{\times}, 4×4{\times}, or 8×8{\times} inference-step budget. As references, we also evaluate the AnyFlow initialisation, from which all seven trainers start, and the pretrained SD3.5-Medium, with the same prompts, seed, resolution and shifted grid. SD3.5-Medium models the instantaneous velocity and is not distilled for few-step sampling, so it uses the Euler step Equation (4) with classifier-free guidance of scale 4.54.5, i.e., two network evaluations per step.

Main results.

Figure 7 shows the per-step trends, and Table S3 in Appendix D reports the percentage changes. We draw four conclusions.

  1. (i)

    Models at different training stages show different test-time scaling behaviour. The pretrained SD3.5-Medium models the instantaneous velocity, so four Euler steps are far too coarse; its scores rise sharply from four to eight steps and keep improving more slowly up to 3232 steps (HPSv3 from −4.49-4.49 to 9.969.96, Figure 7). Even at 3232 steps, i.e., 6464 network evaluations, it remains below every fine-tuned model at four steps in HPSv3, ImageReward, the aesthetic score, HPSv2 and PickScore. In contrast, the AnyFlow initialisation, distilled from SD3.5-Medium for few-step sampling, appears to have already fixed its output patterns at the step count used in training, and its HPSv3, ImageReward and GenEval2 drop markedly with more steps; for example, from 44 to 3232 steps, ImageReward falls from 1.111.11 to 1.021.02 and GenEval2 from 0.3630.363 to 0.3200.320 (Figure 7), beyond the ∼0.03{\sim}0.03 resolution. By comparison, the RL fine-tuned models, which all start from this initialisation, fluctuate less in these three evaluators.

  2. (ii)

    There is no systematic gain on the training reward. Across the fine-tuned models, the three reward summands remain nearly flat (Figure 7 and Table S3). From 44 to 3232 steps, the held-out HPSv3 changes by between +1.0%+1.0\% and −6.8%-6.8\% for six of the seven trainers, compared with −17%-17\% for the AnyFlow initialisation (Figure 7). The stronger degradation of the initialisation itself suggests that the decline in rewards of the fine-tuned models is inherited from the initialisation rather than introduced by RL fine-tuning. Further, these small changes are consistent with the 44-step outputs already having settled into patterns that score well under the training reward, including sampler-specific reward exploitation. Doubling to Mstep=8M_{\mathrm{step}}=8 often preserves or slightly improves a score, but the gain generally saturates or reverses as the grid is refined further. Figure 8 shows both behaviours; MeanFlowAWM improves at eight steps and then declines, whereas ReFL declines gradually.

  3. (iii)

    OCR-sensitive prompts can expose a much sharper failure mode. The selected failures occur on malformed or OCR-heavy prompts. A clear example is shown in Figure 10, where the DMDNFT and MeanFlowNFT samples collapse at Mstep=32M_{\mathrm{step}}=32 to little more than foreground text. HPSv3 falls from 12.1812.18 to 0.320.32 and from 11.3611.36 to 0.320.32, respectively, even as CLIPScore rises from 0.2750.275 to 0.3240.324 and from 0.2920.292 to 0.3090.309. In these selected cases, additional solver steps produce increasingly text-dominated outputs rather than a visual-quality improvement.

  4. (iv)

    Visible sample-level scaling exists. On inspection, many samples improve with 22–44 times as many sampling steps, even though the aggregate rewards barely change; on the selected samples, HPSv3 does rise (Figure 10). At four steps, they have weak clarity or unstable details, while eight or sixteen steps yield cleaner and more stable generations; Figure 10 shows two such cases. The aggregate rewards thus appear less sensitive to these improvements than visual inspection, and test-time scaling may be useful beyond what the aggregate scores suggest, although more steps do not improve quality monotonically.

6.6 Practical Guidance

The empirical results, each from a single run, suggest the following guidance:

  1. (i)

    Where it is affordable, the reward gradient is our recommended approach. Driving the update directly by ∇R\nabla R was the most effective choice in our mixed-reward image experiments; FewStepOPSD and ReFL achieve the two highest training rewards in the mixed-reward setting and improve all three summands (§6.3). However, the applicability of these methods is restricted in practice. (i) The gradient can become too expensive when the reward model and the decoder are large or the latent token sequence is long, as on video (§6.4). (ii) The reward must be differentiable with respect to the clean sample, which excludes OCR accuracy and VideoAlign’s MQ and TA (§6.1, Section D.5). Where both conditions hold, ReFL alone is already a strong baseline in our runs.

  2. (ii)

    Otherwise, group-advantage-based methods apply. When the reward gradient is too expensive or unavailable, the reward enters only through the group advantage, and these methods must convert the average velocity into the instantaneous one (§4.3). Among them, the DMD-based methods, which estimate the instantaneous velocity with the auxiliary network vϕv_{\phi}, have a lower per-iteration cost in the image setting but a higher one on video, depending on the relative cost of the saved forward passes for JJ and the added forward and backward passes of vϕv_{\phi} (§6.3, §6.4). They need extra optimisation steps and memory for vϕv_{\phi}, and in some of the reported runs their larger reward gains coincide with larger held-out degradation.

  3. (iii)

    Among the group-advantage-based methods, the DiffusionNFT family reached high reward values in relatively few iterations. The FlowGRPO-style replay of FewStepGRPO optimises slowly and has the weakest observed reward endpoints within the common iteration budget: it barely improves the mixed reward on images and loses the most reward on video. The DiffusionNFT family reached high reward values within the common iteration budget in both settings, although the cost per iteration varies; MeanFlowNFT is expensive in the image setting and DMDNFT on video. AWM mostly lies between the two in the reported reward outcomes and uses a PPO-style clip to limit each update.

  4. (iv)

    Test-time scaling of the fine-tuned few-step models saturates quickly. Aggregate scores show no systematic gain; three of the seven HPSv3 curves peak at the training step count of four and one is tied between four and eight steps (Table S3). By visual inspection, however, many individual samples look cleaner with 22–44 times as many steps before the effect saturates or reverses. Additional steps therefore improve the visual quality of some samples but do not improve aggregate scores monotonically (§6.5), and can degrade sample quality on OCR-sensitive prompts.

7 Conclusion

Few-step generators reduce the rollout cost that typically dominates RL post-training of diffusion models, but they model an average velocity over an interval, whereas existing RL objectives assume an instantaneous velocity and a many-step sampler. This paper adapts these objectives to few-step models systematically in three phases and compares the resulting methods within one codebase. The transformation to xx-space expresses each objective we consider through a common policy prediction. The decomposition writes the gradient of each objective as the sum of a reward-free self-regression and a reward augmentation, so that a method reduces to a choice of three anchors and three weights. The adaptation computes these anchors from a few-step model, at the end of its transport or along its tangent, with the instantaneous velocity recovered from the network itself through the MeanFlow identity (the self-induced velocity) or from an auxiliary network. The seven resulting trainers share one training step and are compared under shared rollout, reward and evaluation code, each in a single run. Where the reward is differentiable and its gradient affordable, FewStepOPSD and ReFL, which use the reward gradient, were the most effective. Otherwise, the DiffusionNFT family reached high rewards in relatively few iterations, and the DMD-based variants were faster per iteration on image but slower on video, depending on the relative cost of forward and backward passes, and in some runs coincided with larger held-out degradation. For the fine-tuned models, additional sampling steps gave no systematic aggregate gain, although many individual samples improve with two to four times as many steps as in training.

Open problems.

Several questions remain open.

  1. (i)

    The DMD-based variants estimate the instantaneous velocity with an auxiliary network, which requires additional forward and backward passes to fit this network and GPU memory to hold it. How to reduce this overhead remains open.

  2. (ii)

    Reward-gradient-based methods require a reward that is differentiable with respect to the clean sample and a gradient that fits in memory. On video, the motion-quality and text-alignment terms of VideoAlign provide no gradient, and the per-frame decoding required by GPU memory makes the gradient deviate strongly from that of a joint decode. Cheaper and more faithful reward gradients for long latent sequences are needed.

  3. (iii)

    With a scalar group advantage in the mixed-reward setting, whether every reward summand takes effect depends on the weighting of the summands, on the rescaling by the global-batch standard deviation in Equation (83), and on the small within-group spread of some summands (Section D.2). A general and more reliable construction of the group advantage remains open.

  4. (iv)

    In our experiments, a few-step model fine-tuned at one step count does not improve systematically with more steps. Fine-tuning at more step counts may give test-time scaling but makes the rollouts more expensive. Whether it can be introduced cheaply during training, or without training, so that a model fine-tuned at a small step count still improves with more steps at test time, remains open.
