Appendix A Notation

This paper connects several families of methods and therefore uses a large number of symbols. We collect them in the following table; each symbol is also defined where it first appears.

Appendix B FewStepGRPO

Throughout this appendix, (xt,xr)(x_{t},x_{r}) denotes a transition of the stochastic sampler Equation (94) replayed as in §5.3, where t>rt>r are consecutive levels of the rollout grid, Δ​t=t−r\Delta t=t-r, and s∈[0,t]s\in[0,t] is the lower endpoint of the flow map, redrawn at every inner iteration. The same estimate J=J⁡[uold,t,s]J=J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,s\big] is added to both means of Equation (95),

μθ=αt​xt−bt​(uθ​(xt,t,s)+J),μold=αt​xt−bt​(uold​(xt,t,s)+J),\mu_{\theta}=\alpha_{t}\,x_{t}-b_{t}\,\big(u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)+J\big),\qquad\mu_{\mathrm{old}}=\alpha_{t}\,x_{t}-b_{t}\,\big(u_{\mathrm{old}}(x_{t},t,s)+J\big), (108)

where JJ is evaluated by Equation (109), with tangent (xt−x^)/t(x_{t}-\hat{x})/t. Squared norms are per-sample means meansp⁡[⋅]\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\cdot\right], as in Stage 4.

B.1 Why there is no auxiliary-velocity variant

The auxiliary velocity cannot be used for the current prediction, because substituting vϕv_{\phi} would give ∂x~θ/∂θ=0\partial\tilde{x}_{\theta}/\partial\theta=0 (§4.3); the trainers that use vϕv_{\phi} therefore use it only for the baseline, x~base=x~aux\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{aux}} (Equation (60), Equation (104)). In FewStepGRPO, both anchors that an auxiliary field could replace are already fixed, x~reg=∅\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\varnothing and x~base=sg⁡(x~θ)=sg⁡(μθ)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta})=\operatorname{sg}(\mu_{\theta}) (Equation (97)), and §B.3 shows that this choice reproduces the gradient of the tempered Gaussian log-score of the action. Apart from the detached JJ shared by both means, the old policy enters through μold\mu_{\mathrm{old}} in ρ¯GRPO\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}. An auxiliary variant would therefore have to place vϕv_{\phi} inside the scoring kernel.

(a) vϕv_{\phi} as the old-policy field. If μold\mu_{\mathrm{old}} were replaced by μϕ=αt​xt−bt​vϕ​(xt,t)\mu_{\phi}=\alpha_{t}\,x_{t}-b_{t}\,v_{\phi}(x_{t},t), then at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}} the scoring ratio would compare the distances of μϕ\mu_{\phi} and μold\mu_{\mathrm{old}} to xrx_{r}. The ratio would then generally differ from one at zero policy drift, so the PPO clip would respond to the approximation error of vϕv_{\phi} as well as to the change of the policy.

(b) vϕv_{\phi} as the source of the shared correction. Replacing JJ by vϕ​(xt,t)−uold​(xt,t,s)v_{\phi}(x_{t},t)-u_{\mathrm{old}}(x_{t},t,s) in both means of Equation (108) keeps μθ−μold=−bt​(uθ−uold)\mu_{\theta}-\mu_{\mathrm{old}}=-b_{t}\,(u_{\theta}-u_{\mathrm{old}}), hence ρ¯GRPO=1\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}=1 at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, but it requires vϕv_{\phi} at the replayed state xtx_{t}. By Equation (88), vϕv_{\phi} is fitted on re-noised states AddNoise​(x^,t)=(1−t)​x^+t​ϵ\textsc{AddNoise}(\hat{x},t)=(1-t)\hat{x}+t\epsilon, with ϵ\epsilon independent of x^\hat{x}, against the conditional velocity vcond=ϵ−x^v_{\mathrm{cond}}=\epsilon-\hat{x}. A replayed state is not of this form, because Equation (94) adds fresh noise at every step; hence xtx_{t} and the endpoint x^\hat{x} of the same trajectory are not connected by a straight path with independent noise ϵ\epsilon, and vcondv_{\mathrm{cond}} is not defined at xtx_{t}. Exact transport at every step would be sufficient for the two state marginals to agree, but the finite-step map used here is not exact; the replay query can therefore differ from the distribution on which vϕv_{\phi} is fitted. In an earlier run of construction (b), not among those of §6, which queried vϕv_{\phi} at the replayed states, the evaluated OCR accuracy fell from 0.4980.498 to 0.0160.016 within 4040 iterations while the loss Equation (88) decreased from 0.3540.354 to 0.1520.152. This is consistent with vϕv_{\phi} improving on its training distribution while being evaluated on a different one. Querying vϕv_{\phi} at a re-noised state instead removes the mismatch, but the correction is then evaluated at a state other than the one at which the kernel is centred, and the scored density is no longer that of the transition that was taken.

The trainers of §§5.4–5.5 avoid both problems. Their query state AddNoise​(x^,t)\textsc{AddNoise}(\hat{x},t) follows the training distribution of vϕv_{\phi} (Stage 3 (i)), and vϕv_{\phi} enters only through their baseline. FewStepGRPO, whose kernel has to be evaluated at the states the sampler visited, therefore uses only the shared-JJ construction.

B.2 The transition kernel

Replay trajectory.

A state stored on the replay trajectory is not an endpoint-renoise state AddNoise​(x^,t)\textsc{AddNoise}(\hat{x},t), so vcondv_{\mathrm{cond}} is not its tangent. We instead use (xt−x^)/t(x_{t}-\hat{x})/t:

J⁡[uold,t,s]=(t−s)​uold​(xt+εcd​xt−x^t,t+εcd,s)−uold​(xt−εcd​xt−x^t,t−εcd,s)2​εcd.J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,s\big]=(t-s)\,\frac{u_{\mathrm{old}}\!\big(x_{t}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}}\tfrac{x_{t}-\hat{x}}{t},t+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}},s\big)-u_{\mathrm{old}}\!\big(x_{t}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}}\tfrac{x_{t}-\hat{x}}{t},t-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}},s\big)}{2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}}}. (109)

The result is detached and shared by both means. It costs two no-grad forwards of uoldu_{\mathrm{old}}.

Boundary condition.

The coefficients of Equation (95) use the following implemented noise scale on the rollout grid:

ςtj={ς​t01−t1,j=0,ς​tj1−tj,j=1,…,Mstep−1.\varsigma_{t_{j}}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\varsigma\sqrt{\frac{t_{0}}{1-t_{1}}},&j=0,\\[8.0pt] \displaystyle\varsigma\sqrt{\frac{t_{j}}{1-t_{j}}},&j=1,\dots,M_{\mathrm{step}}-1.\end{cases} (110)

The coefficients αt\alpha_{t} and btb_{t} retain the source level t=tjt=t_{j}; only the singular denominator of ςt0\varsigma_{t_{0}} is evaluated at t1t_{1}.

Derivation of Equation (95).

Write σ\sigma for the level along the linear path, on which the probability-flow ODE reads d​xσ=v⁡(xσ,σ)​d​σ\mathrm{d}x_{\sigma}=v(x_{\sigma},\sigma)\,\mathrm{d}\sigma, with vv the marginal velocity, and the score is ∇xσlogpσ(xσ)=−(xσ+(1−σ)v(xσ,σ))/σ\nabla_{x_{\sigma}}\log p_{\sigma}(x_{\sigma})=-\big(x_{\sigma}+(1-\sigma)\,v(x_{\sigma},\sigma)\big)/\sigma (§3, the paragraph on DMD). For any diffusion coefficient ςσ≥0\varsigma_{\sigma}\geq 0, the forward-time SDE

d​xσ=[v⁡(xσ,σ)+12​ςσ2​∇xσ​log⁡pσ​(xσ)]​d​σ+ςσ​d​B\mathrm{d}x_{\sigma}=\Big[v(x_{\sigma},\sigma)+\tfrac{1}{2}\varsigma_{\sigma}^{2}\nabla_{x_{\sigma}}\log p_{\sigma}(x_{\sigma})\Big]\mathrm{d}\sigma+\varsigma_{\sigma}\,\mathrm{d}B (111)

has the same marginals as the probability-flow ODE: in its Fokker–Planck equation, the term −12ςσ2∇⋅(pσ∇logpσ)-\tfrac{1}{2}\varsigma_{\sigma}^{2}\nabla\!\cdot(p_{\sigma}\nabla\log p_{\sigma}) contributed by the added drift and the diffusion term 12​ςσ2​∇2pσ\tfrac{1}{2}\varsigma_{\sigma}^{2}\nabla^{2}p_{\sigma} cancel, since pσ∇logpσ=∇pσp_{\sigma}\nabla\log p_{\sigma}=\nabla p_{\sigma}. The time reversal of Equation (111), run from σ=1\sigma=1 to σ=0\sigma=0, is

d​xσ=[v⁡(xσ,σ)−12​ςσ2​∇xσ​log⁡pσ​(xσ)]​d​σ+ςσ​d​B¯,d​σ<0.\mathrm{d}x_{\sigma}=\Big[v(x_{\sigma},\sigma)-\tfrac{1}{2}\varsigma_{\sigma}^{2}\nabla_{x_{\sigma}}\log p_{\sigma}(x_{\sigma})\Big]\mathrm{d}\sigma+\varsigma_{\sigma}\,\mathrm{d}\bar{B},\qquad\mathrm{d}\sigma<0. (112)

One Euler–Maruyama step from tt to rr, i.e. d​σ=−Δ​t\mathrm{d}\sigma=-\Delta t, followed by the substitution of the score, gives

xr=xt−Δ​t​v−ςt2​Δ​t2​t​(xt+(1−t)​v)+ςt​Δ​t​ξ=(1−ςt2​Δ​t2​t)​xt−(1+ςt2​(1−t)2​t)​Δ​t​v+ςt​Δ​t⏟σk​ξ,\begin{split}x_{r}&=x_{t}-\Delta t\,v-\frac{\varsigma_{t}^{2}\Delta t}{2t}\big(x_{t}+(1-t)v\big)+\varsigma_{t}\sqrt{\Delta t}\,\xi\\ &={\Big(1-\frac{\varsigma_{t}^{2}\Delta t}{2t}\Big)}x_{t}-{\Big(1+\frac{\varsigma_{t}^{2}(1-t)}{2t}\Big)\Delta t}\,v+\underbrace{\varsigma_{t}\sqrt{\Delta t}}_{\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}}\,\xi,\end{split} (113)

with ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), which is Equation (95). The choice Equation (110) of ςt\varsigma_{t}, which avoids the singularity at the source endpoint, fixes the coefficients; at t0=1t_{0}=1 only the denominator of ςt0\varsigma_{t_{0}} is evaluated at t1t_{1}, while αt\alpha_{t} and btb_{t} retain the source level t0t_{0}. The transition density is 𝒩⁡(αt​xt−bt​v,σk2​I)\mathcal{N}(\alpha_{t}\,x_{t}-b_{t}\,v,\ \sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}I), whose mean is affine in vv; moreover, σk>0\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}>0 on every transition of the grid.

Equivalence with the kernel of an instantaneous-velocity policy.

For an average-velocity policy the MeanFlow identity, Equation (6), gives uθ​(xt,t,s)+(t−s)​∂tuθ​(xt,t,s)=vθ​(xt,t)u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)+(t-s)\,\partial_{t}u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)=v_{\theta}(x_{t},t) for every s∈[0,t]s\in[0,t]. If JJ were computed from uθu_{\theta}, the velocity used in Equation (113) would therefore be the instantaneous velocity of the policy, the same for every ss, and the transition density of FewStepGRPO would be that of FlowGRPO for the policy vθv_{\theta}. Computing JJ from uoldu_{\mathrm{old}}, as every v-form trainer does (Stage 3 (ii)), makes this exact at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, up to the error of Equation (109); for θ≠θold\theta\neq\theta_{\mathrm{old}} the field is vθ−(t−s)​∂t(uθ−uold)v_{\theta}-(t-s)\,\partial_{t}(u_{\theta}-u_{\mathrm{old}}), which depends on ss only through a term of the order of the drift of the policy from the old policy. Two consequences follow.

  • •

    ss enters the gradient through the entry of the flow map that is differentiated, ∂μθ/∂θ=−bt∂uθ(xt,t,s)/∂θ\partial\mu_{\theta}/\partial\theta=-b_{t}\,\partial u_{\theta}(x_{t},t,s)/\partial\theta, and the scored density only through that drift term. Redrawing s|ts\mid t at every inner iteration therefore distributes the gradient of one transition over the entries uθ​(⋅,t,s)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,s), s∈[0,t]s\in[0,t], as Stage 3 (i) does for the trainers that re-noise, without changing what is scored at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}.

  • •

    For any objective ℒ⁡(μθ)\mathcal{L}(\mu_{\theta}), ∇θℒ=−bt(∂uθ/∂θ)⊤∂ℒ/∂μθ\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}=-b_{t}\,(\partial u_{\theta}/\partial\theta)^{\top}\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial\mu_{\theta}, since JJ is detached (Equation (41)). This equals the FlowGRPO gradient with ∂vθ/∂θ\partial v_{\theta}/\partial\theta replaced by ∂uθ​(⋅,t,s)/∂θ\partial u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,s)/\partial\theta.

The tempered scoring ratio.

The ratio Equation (96) is the 1/N1/N power of the Gaussian density ratio, equivalently the ratio at temperature N​σk2N\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}.

The tempered ratio at zero drift.

Since the same JJ is added to both means, μθ−μold=−bt​(uθ−uold)​(xt,t,s)\mu_{\theta}-\mu_{\mathrm{old}}=-b_{t}\,(u_{\theta}-u_{\mathrm{old}})(x_{t},t,s), and expanding the two squares of log⁡ρ¯GRPO\log\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}} in Equation (96) gives

log⁡ρ¯GRPO=−btσk2​meansp​[(uθ−uold)⊙(xr−μold)]−bt22​σk2​meansp​[(uθ−uold)2].\log\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}=-\frac{b_{t}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}}\,\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[(u_{\theta}-u_{\mathrm{old}})\odot(x_{r}-\mu_{\mathrm{old}})\right]-\frac{b_{t}^{2}}{2\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}}\,\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[(u_{\theta}-u_{\mathrm{old}})^{2}\right]. (114)

Hence ρ¯GRPO=1\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}=1 at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, regardless of the error of JJ and of the kernel that generated xrx_{r}, because the same JJ enters both means and the same xrx_{r} enters both squares. The ratio differs from one only through uθ−uoldu_{\theta}-u_{\mathrm{old}}.

Relation to the kernel that produced the action.

In the notation of Equation (94), xt=x^tjx_{t}=\hat{x}_{t_{j}} and xr=x^tj+1x_{r}=\hat{x}_{t_{j+1}}, and the action was drawn by the flow-map step to the level sjs_{j} drawn by the sampler, x^sj=x^tj−(tj−sj)​uold​(x^tj,tj,sj)\hat{x}_{s_{j}}=\hat{x}_{t_{j}}-(t_{j}-s_{j})\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\hat{x}_{t_{j}},t_{j},s_{j}), followed by x^tj+1=1−tj+11−sj​x^sj+τj​ϵ′\hat{x}_{t_{j+1}}=\frac{1-t_{j+1}}{1-s_{j}}\,\hat{x}_{s_{j}}+\tau_{j}\epsilon^{\prime}. Given an exact flow-map jump to sjs_{j}, this rollout kernel preserves the linear-path marginal exactly: if x^sj=(1−sj)​x+sj​ϵ\hat{x}_{s_{j}}=(1-s_{j})x+s_{j}\epsilon, then x^tj+1=(1−tj+1)​x+(1−tj+11−sj​sj​ϵ+τj​ϵ′)\hat{x}_{t_{j+1}}=(1-t_{j+1})x+\big(\tfrac{1-t_{j+1}}{1-s_{j}}s_{j}\epsilon+\tau_{j}\epsilon^{\prime}\big), a noise of variance tj+12t_{j+1}^{2} by the definition of τj\tau_{j}. This kernel, however, differs from Equation (113). Its mean is 1−tj+11−sj​(x^tj−(tj−sj)​uold)\frac{1-t_{j+1}}{1-s_{j}}\big(\hat{x}_{t_{j}}-(t_{j}-s_{j})u_{\mathrm{old}}\big) and its width is τj\tau_{j}, with τj=0\tau_{j}=0 whenever sj=tj+1s_{j}=t_{j+1}, in which case the kernel is deterministic and has no likelihood ratio. On the four-step grid, with sjs_{j} drawn uniformly from the remaining grid levels, this happens for 52%52\% of the transitions, including every final transition. FewStepGRPO therefore scores the action under Equation (113), for three reasons: σk>0\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}>0 on every transition; the mean is affine in the instantaneous velocity, so that the equivalence above holds; and the tempered ratio is exact at zero drift by Equation (114). The approximation lies in the scored transition. Besides the noise τj​ϵ′\tau_{j}\epsilon^{\prime}, both xr−μoldx_{r}-\mu_{\mathrm{old}} in Equation (114) and xr−μθx_{r}-\mu_{\theta} in the gradient of §B.3 contain the deterministic difference between the means of the two kernels. Consequently, ρ¯GRPO\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}} is a tempered ratio of the surrogate scoring kernels and not an exact importance ratio for the rollout kernel.

B.3 The decoupled loss

The decoupled loss reproduces the gradient of the tempered clipped surrogate.

Per transition, define

ℒGRPOtemp:=−min⁡{A​ρ¯GRPO,A​clip⁡(ρ¯GRPO,1±εclip)}.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}^{\mathrm{temp}}:=-\min\{A\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}},\ A\operatorname{clip}(\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}},1\pm\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}})\}.

Where the first branch attains the minimum, its gradient is −A​ρ¯GRPO​∇θ​log⁡ρ¯GRPO-A\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}\nabla_{\theta}\log\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}; where the second does, it is constant in θ\theta and contributes no gradient. With the explicit gate χGRPO\chi_{\mathrm{GRPO}} of Equation (96) and the per-element Gaussian log-score sθGRPO:=−meansp[(μθ−xr)2]/(2σk2)s_{\theta}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}:=-\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[(\mu_{\theta}-x_{r})^{2}\right]/(2\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}),

∇θℒGRPOtemp=−χGRPO​A​ρ¯GRPON​σk2​(∂μθ∂θ)⊤​(xr−μθ).\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}^{\mathrm{temp}}=-\frac{\chi_{\mathrm{GRPO}}A\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}}{N\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}}\left(\frac{\partial\mu_{\theta}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\top}\big(x_{r}-\mu_{\theta}\big). (115)

Substituting Equation (97) into Equation (90) gives ℒrwd=W​meansp​[(x~θ−sg⁡(x~θ)−g)2]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}}=W\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\big(\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta})-g\big)^{2}\right] with x~θ=μθ\tilde{x}_{\theta}=\mu_{\theta} and g=ω⁡(xr−sg⁡(μθ))g=\omega\,(x_{r}-\operatorname{sg}(\mu_{\theta})); since x~θ−sg⁡(x~θ)\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}) vanishes in value and has the identity as Jacobian,

∇θℒrwd=−2​W​ωN​(∂μθ∂θ)⊤​(xr−μθ),\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}}=-\frac{2W\omega}{N}\left(\frac{\partial\mu_{\theta}}{\partial\theta}\right)^{\!\top}\big(x_{r}-\mu_{\theta}\big),

which, with W=ρ¯GRPOW=\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}} and ω=χGRPO​A/(2​σk2)\omega=\chi_{\mathrm{GRPO}}A/(2\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}), is Equation (115) term by term. The equality holds for gradients; the value of ℒrwd\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rwd}} is W​meansp​[g2]W\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[g^{2}\right], as for every trainer (Stage 4).

Justification of each factor.

  • •

    The per-element mean. A Gaussian log-density is a sum over the NN non-batch elements of one latent; taking it as the mean meansp⁡[⋅]\operatorname{mean}_{\mathrm{sp}}\!\left[\cdot\right] divides the exponent by NN, which is why ρ¯GRPO\bar{\rho}_{\mathrm{GRPO}} is the 1/N1/N power of the density ratio, or equivalently a score at temperature N​σk2N\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}. Here N=65,536N=65{,}536 for the image latent and N=2,096,640N=2{,}096{,}640 for the video latent. Using the mean keeps the ratio within floating-point range (with the sum, the exponent can overflow for differences allowed by the clip), follows FlowGRPO, and is consistent with a clipping radius of order 10−310^{-3}.

  • •

    The factor 1/(2​σk2)1/(2\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}) in ω\omega. The reward term of Equation (90) contributes 2​W​ω/N2W\omega/N times the displacement, so ω\omega must contain the factor 1/(2​σk2)1/(2\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}) of the log-score for Equation (115) to hold. Without it, each transition would be weighted by 2​σk22\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}, which varies by a factor of 2.72.7 across the four transitions of the grid; a single learning rate cannot compensate for such a transition-dependent scale.

  • •

    x~base=sg⁡(x~θ)\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\operatorname{sg}(\tilde{x}_{\theta}). The score of the Gaussian at the action, (xr−μθ)/σk2(x_{r}-\mu_{\theta})/\sigma_{\mathrm{k}}^{2}, is measured from the current mean, so the origin of the reward direction has to follow the policy. A fixed origin μold\mu_{\mathrm{old}}, i.e. a translation as in DiffusionNFT, coincides with it only at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}.

  • •

    x~reg=∅\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\varnothing. The self-regression role is played by the ratio and its clip, and by the velocity penalty of Equation (92); a self-regression term would add to Equation (115) a gradient that the policy-gradient estimator does not contain.

  • •

    Method-specific cadvc_{\mathrm{adv}} scaling. The implemented NFT and general OPSD trainers multiply both loss weights WW by cadvc_{\mathrm{adv}} to undo the compression of Equation (84); the factor is written explicitly in Equation (106) and Equation (107). ReFL keeps it although it fixes r^≡1\hat{r}\equiv 1. FewStepGRPO does not use it, since ω\omega already contains the gated signed advantage χGRPO​A\chi_{\mathrm{GRPO}}A.

Appendix C FewStepOPSD

This appendix proves that, in the v-form of §5.6, the loss and its gradient do not depend on the detached term JJ. After dropping JJ, the current prediction and its anchors reduce to the JJ-free (t,r)(t,r) query of §4.3, i.e., the average velocity queried at (t,r)(t,r) and transported to the clean end without correction, while the reward-gradient steps still start from the r=0r=0 prediction. We follow one member and suppress the index (i)(i). Every prediction is evaluated at the query state x~t\tilde{x}_{t} of level tt and at the rr drawn during the reward-coupled construction and reused at fitting (§5.6, (i)). Four properties of the implementation are used:

  1. (a)

    the same detached estimate J=J⁡[uold,t,r]J=J\big[u_{\mathrm{old}},\,t,\,r\big] is added to every prediction (Stage 3 (iii));

  2. (b)

    the old policy uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} is the same in the reward-coupled construction and in fitting, being refreshed only after the policy update of the outer iteration (Stage 1);

  3. (c)

    the points x~±\tilde{x}_{\pm} are constructed by Equation (70); the gradient steps start from the r=0r=0 prediction, and only the resulting displacement is added to the anchor;

  4. (d)

    the velocity penalty, where present, is that of Equation (92).

C.1 The quantities

By Equation (86) and Equation (69), the current prediction and the anchors are

x~θ\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\theta} =x~t−t⁡(uθ​(x~t,t,r)+J),\displaystyle=\tilde{x}_{t}-t\big(u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)+J\big), (116)
x~reg=x~base,1=x~base,2=x~ind\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base},1}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base},2}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}} =x~t−t⁡(uold​(x~t,t,r)+J).\displaystyle=\tilde{x}_{t}-t\big(u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r)+J\big).

Corollary C.3.

Dropping JJ in Equation (116) gives

x~θ=X[x~t,uθ(x~t,t,r), 0],x~reg=x~base=x~ind|J=0=X[x~t,uold(x~t,t,r), 0],x~±=x~base+Δrwd​x~±,\begin{gathered}\tilde{x}_{\theta}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\theta}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big],\qquad\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}={\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}|_{J=0}}=X\big[\tilde{x}_{t},\,u_{\mathrm{old}}(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r),\,0\big],\\ \tilde{x}_{\pm}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}+\Delta_{\mathrm{rwd}}\tilde{x}_{\pm},\end{gathered}

These are the JJ-free (t,r)(t,r) queries of §4.3; they coincide with the u-form quantities of §5.6 (ii) except that the current prediction and its anchors are queried at (t,r)(t,r) instead of (t,0)(t,0); the reward displacement is still computed from x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}. At r=0r=0 the two constructions coincide, since then x~base=x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}=\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}} and Δ=0\Delta=0. Freeing rr therefore trains every uθ​(⋅,t,r)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,r) while the decoder and the reward gradient are still evaluated at the clean prediction x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}; the u-form trains only uθ​(⋅,t,0)u_{\theta}(\cdot,t,0).

C.3 Remarks

Remark C.4 (The cancellation as a translation).

Steps 1–4 state that JJ shifts the five points x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta}, x~reg\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}, x~base\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}, x~+\tilde{x}_{+}, x~−\tilde{x}_{-} by the same detached vector −t​J-tJ (with x~±\tilde{x}_{\pm} shifted through the offset Δ\Delta of Equation (70)), whereas the loss depends on them only through x~θ−x~reg\tilde{x}_{\theta}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}} and x~±−x~base\tilde{x}_{\pm}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}}. The two quantities of the construction that depend on an absolute position, the points at which ∇R\nabla R is evaluated and the radius of the trust region, are evaluated at x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}}, which does not depend on JJ.

Remark C.5 (Where the cancellation fails).

(i) If the gradient steps were started at x~ind\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}} itself instead of at x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}} as prescribed by Equation (70), ∇R\nabla R would be evaluated at, and the radius computed from, points displaced by −t​J-tJ, and JJ would remain in Δrwd​x~±\Delta_{\mathrm{rwd}}\tilde{x}_{\pm}; this is why Example 8 (iii) starts the steps at the JJ-free prediction. (ii) If the constructed points were left at the end point of the iteration, x~±[Mtgt]\tilde{x}^{[M_{\mathrm{tgt}}]}_{\pm}, instead of being shifted back by Δ\Delta, the differences x~±−x~base\tilde{x}_{\pm}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}} would contain Δ\Delta and hence JJ. (iii) The penalty of Equation (93) contains JJ in its target. (iv) An old policy refreshed between point construction and fitting would make x~base\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{base}} at fitting differ from the anchor around which x~±\tilde{x}_{\pm} were placed, by a term that the cancellation does not remove.

Remark C.6 (Why the argument does not extend to the other trainers).

In FewStepNFT, FewStepAWM and FewStepGRPO the rewarded point is a sample (the rollout sample x^\hat{x} or the action xrx_{r}) and does not contain JJ, whereas the baseline does. Dropping JJ changes the reward displacement of FewStepNFT, g=ω⁡(x^−x~ind)g=\omega(\hat{x}-\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}), by −ω​t​J-\omega\,tJ (Stage 3 (iii)), and the residual xr−μθx_{r}-\mu_{\theta} of FewStepGRPO by −bt​J-b_{t}\,J. This shift can be large; for MeanFlowNFT, the logged mean of |t​J||tJ| is 2.72.7 in the mixed-reward setting and 3.63.6 in the OCR setting, compared with a root-mean-square entry of the clean latent of 1.061.06 and 1.461.46, respectively. In FewStepOPSD, both ends of every reward displacement are constructed from the same anchor, and the gradient steps start from the JJ-free prediction x~old,u\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{old},\mathrm{u}} (Equation (70)); together, these two properties give the cancellation. The same holds for ReFL, whose single reward square is the first one of Equation (68).

C.4 Cost, and an empirical check

JJ requires one directional-difference estimate Equation (87), i.e. two no-grad forwards of uoldu_{\mathrm{old}}. With JJ retained, the v-form evaluates it twice per member and outer iteration: in the reward-coupled construction, to form x~ind\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{ind}}, where the members are processed in micro-batches of six members to bound the memory of the reward backward pass; and in fitting, to form x~θ\tilde{x}_{\theta} and x~reg\tilde{x}_{\mathrm{reg}}. By Corollary C.3 neither evaluation is needed. Table S1 compares two runs of the v-form that differ only in this respect, and the same pair for ReFL with ∇R\nabla R of the full reward. The training reward agrees to within 0.0020.002 for the v-form at every evaluated iteration, and to within 0.0060.006 for ReFL at iteration 400400, below the 1%1\% (about 0.0160.016) by which two evaluation draws of one checkpoint may differ; held-out OCR accuracy differs more.

Appendix D Supplementary Experiments

D.1 Shared hyperparameters

The following values are shared by every trainer of §6.1 and §6.2 and complement the settings listed there.

Old-policy EMA.

The old policy uoldu_{\mathrm{old}} is refreshed once per outer iteration ii by θold←ηi​θold+(1−ηi)​θ\theta_{\mathrm{old}}\leftarrow\eta_{i}\,\theta_{\mathrm{old}}+(1-\eta_{i})\,\theta, with the decay schedule of the official DiffusionNFT implementation (Zheng et al., 2026a): the decay ratio ηi=min⁡{10−3​i, 0.5}\eta_{i}=\min\{10^{-3}i,\,0.5\} increases linearly with the outer iteration ii to a cap of 0.50.5. Since ηi>0\eta_{i}>0 for i≥1i\geq 1, the condition θold=θ\theta_{\mathrm{old}}=\theta of Example 9 holds only at the first outer iteration.

Floors.

The floors are: the residual-scale floor τmin=10−2\tau_{\min}=10^{-2} of FewStepAWM (Equation (101)), the directional-difference step εcd=5×10−3\varepsilon_{\mathrm{cd}}=5\times 10^{-3} (Equation (87)), the adaptive-normaliser floor εγ=10−5\varepsilon_{\gamma}=10^{-5} (Equation (105)), the reward-gradient-norm floor εg=10−12\varepsilon_{g}=10^{-12} (Equation (62)) and the advantage standard-deviation floor εstd=10−4\varepsilon_{\mathrm{std}}=10^{-4} (Equation (83)).

GenEval2.

Following MeanFlowNFT (Huang et al., 2026b), we adopt the official GenEval2 evaluation setting (Kamath et al., 2025).

D.2 Analysis of no gain in CLIPScore for group-advantage runs

In the mixed-reward setting, all five default group-advantage runs end below the pre-RL CLIPScore. The two runs with the full reward gradient instead increase CLIPScore at every listed 100100-iteration checkpoint, to 0.32170.3217 and 0.31720.3172. In contrast, all three CLIP-focused MeanFlowNFT ablations in the lower block of Table S4 end above the pre-RL value.

The training reward weights its three summands equally, but CLIPScore varies little within a prompt group, where the advantage is computed; at the pre-RL policy, its within-group standard deviation is only about 0.010.01 (0.0100.010 and 0.0140.014 on the first iteration of the two CLIPScore-only runs below), roughly a quarter of its global-batch standard deviation and 3.53.5–5%5\% of its value. It accounts for 30.4%30.4\% of the variance of the three summands, against 53.6%53.6\% for PickScore and 16.0%16.0\% for HPSv2, so an equal weight does not give it an equal share of the signal.

We therefore tested three ways of changing that share, the first two on MeanFlowNFT (Table S4, lower block). (i) Raising the weight of CLIPScore: the weights (wCLIP,wHPS,wPick)=(2.4,0.3,0.3)(w_{\mathrm{CLIP}},w_{\mathrm{HPS}},w_{\mathrm{Pick}})=(2.4,0.3,0.3), i.e. 8:1:18{:}1{:}1, and (3.0,0,0)(3.0,0,0), CLIPScore alone, the limit of an unbounded relative weight; both keep K=24K=24. (ii) Enlarging the group: CLIPScore alone with K=72K=72 images per prompt instead of 2424. (iii) Removing it from the gradient: ReFL differentiating HPSv2 alone. The first two increase CLIPScore, and the increase grows with its share; by iteration 400400, it gains 0.01330.0133 at 8:1:18{:}1{:}1, 0.01910.0191 with CLIPScore alone, and 0.03630.0363 with K=72K=72, more than either gradient-based trainer (0.02860.0286–0.03310.0331), although this run draws three times as many images per prompt. In all three runs, however, the other two summands stop improving, and HPSv2 and PickScore oscillate within [0.2473, 0.2974][0.2473,\,0.2974] and [0.8459, 0.8691][0.8459,\,0.8691], the range they occupy at the start of training; under CLIPScore alone the held-out aesthetic score and OCR accuracy also decrease, by 0.640.64–0.980.98 and 0.180.18–0.190.19. Conversely, ReFL with the gradient of HPSv2 alone leaves CLIPScore near its pre-RL value (0.28440.2844–0.28830.2883 over iterations 100100–400400) while raising HPSv2 to 0.39460.3946, the highest of any reported variant.

In these ablations, increasing CLIPScore under a scalar advantage coincides with the gains of the other summands weakening or vanishing. The scalar is shared according to the covariance of each summand with the group reward, so reweighting redistributes the observed signal. The reward gradient instead contains a direction from every summand; in the reported FewStepOPSD and ReFL runs, CLIPScore, HPSv2 and PickScore rise together by 0.02860.0286–0.03310.0331, approximately 0.07050.0705–0.07640.0764, and approximately 0.07380.0738–0.08180.0818, respectively. As noted in the main text, this approach requires a reward that is differentiable with respect to the clean sample.

Conclusion.

In the reported group-advantage ablations, raising the share of CLIPScore or enlarging the group raises CLIPScore while the gains of the other summands are reduced or vanish. In these runs, the weighting of the summands therefore affects which rewards improve, not only how fast they improve. Reward-gradient-based methods provide a direction from every summand, and all three summands rise together in the reported runs; however, these methods apply only when the reward is differentiable with respect to the clean sample, which excludes the OCR setting (§6).

D.3 Why FewStepOPSD resembles ReFL

In FewStepOPSD, the signed reward coefficients satisfy |ω1|+|ω2|=1/β|\omega_{1}|+|\omega_{2}|=1/\beta; r^\hat{r} redistributes this magnitude between the ascent and descent terms and can also change their common weight WW (Equation (107)). Both terms move the prediction in the direction of increasing reward, because g1=ω1​Δrwd​x~+g_{1}=\omega_{1}\Delta_{\mathrm{rwd}}\tilde{x}_{+} and g2=ω2​Δrwd​x~−g_{2}=\omega_{2}\Delta_{\mathrm{rwd}}\tilde{x}_{-} with ω2≤0\omega_{2}\leq 0, while the two increments follow +∇R+\nabla R and −∇R-\nabla R, respectively. The logged mean magnitudes |ω1|=5.12|\omega_{1}|=5.12 and |ω2|=4.88|\omega_{2}|=4.88 differ by 0.240.24, i.e. 2.4%2.4\% of their fixed sum 1/β=101/\beta=10; they do not by themselves determine the imbalance of the two reward-augmentation vectors. FewStepOPSD is therefore close to the ReFL reward augmentation of Example 9, with an added self-regression, a descent term and several gradient steps; this is consistent with the similar curves in Figure 4.

D.4 The velocity penalty: KL-u against KL-v

The velocity penalty, labelled KL in the run names although it is a squared velocity residual (§5.2), admits two constructions: the fixed initial average-velocity reference of Equation (92), which compares uθu_{\theta} and urefu_{\mathrm{ref}} at the same (x~t,t,r)(\tilde{x}_{t},t,r) (KL-u), and the frozen instantaneous teacher of Equation (93), converted through J⁡[uold,t,r]J[u_{\mathrm{old}},t,r], which depends on the old policy (KL-v). The variants therefore differ in both reference construction and parameterisation space, and the weight is 10−410^{-4} in both; the main text reports KL-u under the name MeanFlowNFT.

In the mixed-reward setting, the two variants are close at iteration 400400; both reach a training reward of 1.5091.509, and the held-out evaluators differ by about 11–1.5%1.5\% in either direction (HPSv3 13.2313.23 against 13.3613.36, ImageReward 1.3851.385 against 1.3651.365), with neither variant ahead on both. GenEval2 is 0.4070.407 against 0.4000.400 at iteration 400400. Its average over iterations 100100–400400 is 0.3930.393 against 0.3650.365; the 0.0280.028 gap is near the stated ∼0.03{\sim}0.03 resolution, so we do not interpret it as a clear difference.

In the OCR setting, KL-u reaches OCR accuracy 0.850.85 earlier, at iteration 100100 instead of 150150, with 0.7850.785, 0.8500.850, 0.9450.945 at iterations 5050, 100100, 150150 (the values of Table 6a) against 0.6930.693, 0.8340.834, 0.8970.897. At matched OCR accuracy the difference is mixed; at the first saved checkpoint with OCR accuracy of at least 0.820.82, HPSv3 is 10.6410.64 against 10.2410.24 and ImageReward 0.8870.887 against 0.8960.896, each variant ahead on one of the two. At this weight, the choice of reference therefore has a limited effect in these runs; it changes the iteration at which the OCR threshold is reached but has no clear effect on the quality at that point, and both variants have nearly the same cost per iteration (435435 against 436436 s in the mixed-reward setting). The main text therefore reports only KL-u.

D.5 Partial differentiability of the video reward

This restriction does not occur in the image setting and affects only FewStepOPSD and ReFL.

Every method is evaluated on the same four-term reward. A method that requires ∇R\nabla R can only use the differentiable terms, which on this backbone are HPSv3-general (39%39\% of the sum) and HPSv3-percentile (57%57\%); VideoAlign MQ (6%6\%) and TA (−2%-2\%) are not differentiable. The FewStepOPSD and ReFL runs in Table 8 use the gradients of both HPSv3 reductions, together 96%96\% of the aggregate under the logged normalisation, but no gradient of motion quality or text alignment. On SD3.5, the gradient covers 100%100\% of the training reward, since all three summands are differentiable image scorers.

This restriction is not visible in the reported scalar rewards, since the reward, the online evaluation and the advantage of FewStepOPSD all use the full four-term scorer (ReFL has no advantage). The restriction affects the direction of the gradient and not necessarily the norm of the update.

The released bfloat16 HPSv3 scorer changes the reward value by only ∼0.003{\sim}0.003 relative to fp32 but rotates its gradient by 76.276.2 degrees on average. The runs in Table 8 therefore use fp32 with the sdpa attention backend, so this bf16 error does not affect the reported results. One remaining constraint is that the clip is decoded one latent frame at a time to limit memory; since the VAE is causal, a frame decoded alone is treated as the first frame of a clip. Compared with a joint decode of the same two frames, the gradient deviates by 79.279.2 degrees, and the gradient of the second frame is nearly orthogonal to the joint-decode reference.

The FewStepOPSD and ReFL rows of Table 8 therefore use the gradient of the two HPSv3 terms with per-frame decoding, and not the gradient of the full reward. Removing the causal-decode constraint requires a joint window of at least two frames, which needs 126.1126.1 GB of GPU memory without activation offloading on a 144144 GB card with 25.625.6 GB already in use, or 189189 s per iteration with offloading. Across 4848 GPUs and 250250 iterations this amounts to 26.2526.25 GPU-days (about 0.5470.547 days of wall-clock time if fully parallel). This limitation comes from the memory of a single GPU and not from the method.
